#3166. AI-Driven Tech Layoffs Could Trigger a 1.6 Million Job Recession

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

With more than 200,000 job cuts in the tech industry in 2026, the bigger question is if layoffs will spread to retail and finance.

When Meta began laying off 8,000 people in May, it felt like an omen. Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, had seen several high-profile failures, from the death of the metaverse to its multibillion-dollar court setbacks. The Magnificent Seven — the tech giants that drive US stock market gains — seemed to hit a plateau over the last year, as more investors expressed concern about a potential AI bubble.

A wave of recent tech layoffs and buyouts reveals a growing volatility in the tech industry, as major companies restructure to cut costs and redirect spending toward AI. In just the last few weeks, Google extended its voluntary buyout program to select employees in five countries, and the graphic design platform Canva reduced its staff by 22%, laying off or relocating 1,271 employees.

Companies that have laid off or offered buyouts to 1,000 or more employees this year include Microsoft (60,000), Oracle (21,000), Amazon (17,000 in addition to 14,000 in 2025), Uber (3,300) and Netflix (1,000). According to the TrueUp tech layoffs tracker, layoffs are accelerating faster than last year, with over 200,000 workers reduced so far in 2026. The cuts aren’t limited to struggling companies, but are affecting profitable organizations with strong revenues.

The dominant factor behind layoffs has been AI. Companies have spent billions of dollars on the technology, plus a terrifying $3.2 trillion (with a “T”) that, Goldman Sachs says, doesn’t show up on balance sheets. With current returns failing to justify the massive scale of capital expenditure, companies are slashing labor costs and relying on AI to offset the resulting productivity losses.

While the US isn’t officially in a recession (yet), there are growing fears that mass layoffs could spread to other sectors, such as retailers and financial companies, creating a large wave of workforce reductions in the country. Analysts warn that if job losses extend beyond the tech industry, it could result in another 1.6 million people being laid off, bringing the formal unemployment rate closer to recession-level.

With several economic pressures at play — inflation, higher interest rates and rising energy and computing costs — buyouts and layoffs allow company executives to reduce operating expenses while investing heavily in AI infrastructure, automation and specialized technical talent. That hasn’t worked out in all cases. A handful of companies, including Salesforce and Ford, ended up rehiring or hiring new people after AI-driven layoffs.

Even companies currently reducing their workforce, such as Canva, appear to be offering friendly terms, potentially to avoid burning bridges. As part of its severance package, Canva gave outgoing employees $10,000 grants, MacBooks, six months of salary and a year of healthcare. For many workers without a union contract, that will be the best-case scenario if the economy goes south.

Canva’s terms for departing employees are both exceedingly generous and a window into modern tech:* Six months salary* A year healthcare* A year of LinkedIn premium* A $10k grant to start a business* Keep your MacBook https://t.co/Hqdegdb8Ek pic.twitter.com/pKuj8lJDvB

Job instability, stagnant wages and rising prices have been the norm for several years, arguably since the last major US recession in 2020, at the start of the pandemic. Given that recessions historically occur about every six years (regardless of which party is in the White House), a larger downturn could be on the horizon, especially if an AI market correction triggers further stock declines and widespread layoffs. If high-cost data centers lose clients and major IPOs falter, enterprises will likely slash spending and jobs as the promise of AI-driven efficiency fades.

So far, layoffs don’t appear to be spreading to other industries, and overall job cuts are the lowest since 2022. But the job market has become increasingly precarious, especially for younger workers, according to Lisa Countryman-Quiroz, CEO of JVS Bay Area, a workforce nonprofit.

For example, entry-level hires are down by a third in the most AI-exposed occupations since 2021, which could affect sectors like retail and finance —typical entry-level gateways for many young people. Household wages aren’t keeping up with expenses, and many job seekers have found themselves unemployed for more than six months. “While we may or may not see broadening layoffs, I’m concerned about the erosion of stable career pathways,” Countryman-Quiroz said. The one bright spot seems to be in healthcare, with 42,000 jobs added last month.

The 2026 midterm elections could also indirectly affect tech layoffs, mainly due to changes in the political and regulatory environment around AI and data centers. In the lead-up to the midterms, the backlash against data centers and tech billionaires became a pressing issue for candidates. Campaigns around data center moratoriums helped some Democratic candidates, including Gina Hinojosa, the surprise gubernatorial winner in Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has his home and business headquarters.

Pausing new data center construction will be a shot in the arm for communities protesting the drain of AI infrastructure on local resources. But any slowdown in the buildout could also reduce demand for construction, chip suppliers or technical roles tied to AI expansion.

The midterm elections also affected financial markets, with technology and AI-linked stocks falling as investors worried that Democrats might impose new guardrails on AI. A weaker market can often make companies more cautious about hiring, capital spending and staffing, which could exacerbate cost-cutting pressures and lead to more layoffs and buyouts.

Countryman-Quiroz suggested that Congress could address AI’s disruption by investing in more job training, especially in growing areas like healthcare. “Current federal funding is only sufficient to train about 200,000 workers per year, a fraction of what’s needed,” she said. “Workforce development has historically enjoyed bipartisan support, so there is an opportunity for both parties to work together on solutions.”

#3165. Crescent Capital BDC (CCAP) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Buyback and new joint venture unveiled as watch list ticks higher.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Management reported that Crescent Capital BDC, Inc. (CCAP +12.34%) achieved stable net asset value while introducing multiple capital allocation initiatives focused on deleveraging and addressing its stock price discount. The company announced a $50 million share repurchase program and a separate $25 million purchase commitment from parent company Sun Life. To facilitate these actions and return to target leverage ranges, the company is forming a new $150 million joint venture to be seeded with performing first lien assets. Management indicated that despite subdued buyout volume in the broader market, the company maintained improved interest coverage across its diversified portfolio of 190 companies.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to Crescent Capital BDC, Inc.'s Third Quarter ended September 30, 2026, Earnings Conference Call. Please note that Crescent Capital BDC, Inc. may be referred to as CCAP, Crescent BDC or the company throughout the call. I'll start with some important reminders. Comments made over the course of this conference call and webcast may contain forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties. The company's actual results could differ materially from those expressed in such forward-looking statements for any reason, including those listed in its SEC filings. The company assumes no obligation to update any such forward-looking statements. Please also note that past performance or market information is not a guarantee of future results.

I'll now turn the call over to Dan McMahon.

Daniel McMahon: Thank you. Yesterday after the market closed, the company issued its earnings press release for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, and posted a presentation to the Investor Relations section of its website at www.crescentbdc.com. The presentation should be reviewed in conjunction with the company's Form 10-Q filed yesterday with the SEC. As a reminder, this call is being recorded for replay purposes. Speaking on today's call will be CCAP's Chief Executive Officer, Jason Breaux; Chief Financial Officer, Gerhard Lombard; and President, Henry Chung. With that, I'd now like to turn it over to Jason.

Jason Breaux: Thank you, Dan, and good morning, everyone. I'll begin by reviewing our third quarter results, touch on the current market environment and then outline our key priorities and some of the actions we're announcing today. For the third quarter, we reported net investment income of $0.37 per share, an increase from $0.36 per share in the prior quarter. Our earnings exceeded our $0.34 base dividend, and we also paid the second of our 3 previously announced special dividends of $0.03 per share during the quarter. Our net asset value remained largely stable at $17.72 per share as of September 30 compared with $17.82 at the end of the prior quarter. No new investments were placed on nonaccrual during the quarter.

Turning to the market. Sponsor-backed M&A remained subdued during the third quarter. Direct lending volumes supporting leveraged buyouts was down roughly 21% from the prior quarter and 60% from the third quarter of last year. While limited new buyout activity has moderated new platform financing opportunities and delayed some realizations, demand continues through add-on acquisitions, refinancings and other needs within existing sponsored portfolios. Add-on financings remain an important source of activity for Crescent. Our private credit platform includes more than 250 lower middle market portfolio companies, providing a foundation for originations beyond new LBO transactions. Over the last 12 months, add-on financings accounted for approximately 50% of Crescent's total deal count and 25% of total dollars committed.

Competition for attractive credit remains even as portions of the nontraded BDC market continue to face redemption pressure. In this environment, our long-standing sponsor relationships and familiarity with existing borrowers allow us to remain selective on credit quality, structure and pricing. Despite subdued new activity, the Crescent private credit platform remained active, committing approximately $1.5 billion of capital during the third quarter. As we emphasized last quarter, CCAP remains an important part of Crescent's private credit platform. The permanent fee reductions implemented earlier this year demonstrate Crescent's economic commitment to those objectives. And today, we're building on that commitment with several actions designed to drive NAV accretion by capturing the current discount in our stock.

First, our Board has authorized a $50 million share repurchase program for the purpose of repurchasing shares of our common stock in the open market at certain thresholds below our net asset value per share in accordance with applicable law. We believe our current share price materially undervalues CCAP, making repurchases at substantial discounts to NAV a compelling use of available capital. In addition to the CCAP repurchase program, Crescent's parent entity, Sun Life, will purchase up to an additional $25 million of shares in the open market at certain thresholds below our net asset value per share in accordance with applicable law.

This commitment underscores Sun Life's confidence in CCAP's long-term value and further strengthens the alignment of Sun Life, Crescent and the leadership team with CCAP's shareholders. The timing, manner, price and amount of any share repurchases under the CCAP repurchase program and the Sun Life purchase program will be determined by the company and Sun Life, respectively, in their respective discretion, based upon the evaluation of economic and market conditions, stock price, applicable legal and regulatory requirements and other factors. In order to accelerate share repurchase activity, we expect to announce the formation of an unconsolidated joint venture. The joint venture is expected to be seeded with approximately $150 million of performing first lien assets from CCAP.

CCAP expects to commit $30 million of equity to the joint venture, along with a $30 million expected equity contribution from the joint venture equity partner. In addition to the equity contributions, the joint venture is expected to be capitalized with an ABL facility. We are targeting a low to mid-teens ROE at the joint venture, which we expect to be accretive to our gross yield. The joint venture is expected to be completed during the fourth quarter of 2026. CCAP expects to use the proceeds from the JV to reduce leverage to our target range and fund share repurchases. Together, we believe these actions support our deleveraging objectives and create opportunities for per share accretion.

Finally, I'd like to highlight a recent announcement regarding Crescent's broader platform. On October 26, Sun Life announced GreenOak, a unified global brand, bringing together Crescent, BGO, InfraRed Capital Partners, SLC Fixed Income and Advisors Asset Management. The platform represents approximately $326 billion in assets under management across credit, real estate and infrastructure, supported by a global distribution network. The brand transition will take place over the next 12 months. On the fixed income side, GreenOak brings together Crescent's alternative credit expertise and SLC Fixed Income's investment-grade public and private credit capabilities, providing a broader range of investment solutions and opportunities for collaboration. For CCAP, our investment processes, investment committees and investment personnel remain unchanged.

We will continue to manage the portfolio with the same disciplined underwriting approach and focus on income generation and capital preservation, supported by the resources and reach of the broader GreenOak platform. With that, I'll turn the call over to Gerhard to review our third quarter financial results in more detail. Gerhard?

Gerhard Lombard: Thanks, Jason, and hello, everyone. Net investment income was $0.37 per share for the third quarter, up from $0.36 in the second quarter and covered our $0.34 per share regular dividend. Compared to the second quarter, total investment income increased by approximately $0.6 million to $36.9 million. Interest income increased by approximately $0.9 million to $35.6 million. This was offset by lower dividend income, which declined to approximately $0.9 million from $1.2 million, primarily reflecting lower distributions from the legacy Logan JV as the vehicle continues to run off and deleverage, as discussed in prior quarters.

Total expenses and excise taxes remained stable at $23.2 million with modestly higher financing costs, offset by lower income and excise taxes and professional fees. Turning to the balance sheet. Our investment portfolio totaled approximately $1.6 billion at fair value as of September 30. Total net assets were $653 million or $17.72 per share. On Slide 9, we provide a graphical analysis of the quarter-over-quarter change in NAV. We recorded $0.06 per share of net realized losses, largely offset by reversals of previously recognized unrealized losses on those investments. Net unrealized depreciation, including these reversals, totaled $0.04 per share. Valuation movements reflected slight spread widening, while company-specific credit movements were broadly neutral.

Overall, portfolio valuations were generally stable with NAV per share changing from $17.82 to $17.72. Let's shift to our capitalization and liquidity. I'm on Slide 18. Our debt-to-equity ratio remained 1.42x or 1.36x net of balance sheet cash compared with 1.37x net in the prior quarter. Gross debt outstanding declined to approximately $924 million from $935 million. And cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash totaled approximately $36 million at quarter end. While leverage ended the quarter above our long-term target range, we continue to maintain sufficient liquidity with approximately $247 million of cash and available borrowing capacity as of quarter end.

We expect that pending portfolio realizations and the previously discussed joint venture will bring net leverage to within our target range by year-end. Our Board declared a fourth quarter dividend of $0.34 per share. We will also pay the third and final previously announced special dividend of $0.03 per share on December 15. Our supplemental dividend framework remains in effect, although no supplemental dividend is payable for the quarter under that framework. And with that, I'll turn it over to Henry to discuss the portfolio.

Henry Chung: Thanks, Gerhard. We ended the quarter with approximately $1.6 billion of investments at fair value across 190 portfolio companies. The portfolio remained highly diversified with an average investment size of approximately 0.5% and 91% invested in senior first lien loans. The broader portfolio continues to perform generally in line with our underwriting expectations, with the majority of portfolio companies demonstrating resilient operating performance and year-over-year EBITDA growth. Approximately 84% of investments remained rated 1 or 2, indicating performance at or above expectations. Our weighted average portfolio risk rating remained at 2.1 and weighted average interest coverage improved to 2.3x. Turning to Slide 16.

Our watch list increased modestly from 15% to 16% of the portfolio at fair value, driven by 3-rated investments increasing from 12% to 13%. Investments rated 4 and 5 declined from approximately 3% to 2.4%. We had no new nonaccruals during the quarter. Nonaccruals declined from 4.8% to 4.7% of debt investments at cost, reflecting the sale of a small legacy First Eagle investment previously on nonaccrual. Measured against the total investment portfolio at cost, nonaccruals were 4.4%. Moving to investment activity, with leverage currently above our target range, our new investment activity was limited during the third quarter in order to prioritize deleveraging.

Gross deployment totaled $24 million, the majority of which consisted of follow-on investments in existing portfolio companies. Aggregate exits, sales and repayments totaled approximately $39 million, resulting in net realizations of approximately $15 million for the quarter. With that, I'll turn it back to Jason for closing remarks.

Jason Breaux: Thank you, Henry. Before we open the call for questions, I'd like to leave you with a few closing thoughts. Our primary focus remains the rotation of our watch list. The work remains ongoing and active portfolio management remains a critical component of driving strong recovery outcomes over the long term. Crescent's alignment with our shareholders has been a critical component of how we manage CCAP. Today's $50 million share repurchase authorization and separate $25 million investment by Sun Life build on the permanent fee reductions implemented earlier this year. These initiatives demonstrate the continued commitment of Crescent and Sun Life to CCAP. Finally, we look forward to the opportunities for greater collaboration across the GreenOak platform.

A unified market approach, combined with the continuity of Crescent's investment teams and disciplined investment processes, positions us to build on more than 3 decades of private credit experience for the benefit of CCAP's shareholders. On behalf of the entire Crescent team, I'd like to thank our shareholders for their continued support and confidence. Operator, we'd now be happy to take your questions.

Christopher Nolan: And if I may, just one last one. Your average debt portfolio yields are 9.6%, which tends to be on the low end of the spectrum for BDCs. Is the JV part of a strategy to raise that average portfolio yield?

Finian O'Shea: I'll stick with the JV. Can you give some color on the sort of quantum and nature of assets that you'll drop down in the beginning and the sort of mix of old and new origination that are planned to ramp it?

Henry Chung: Fin, this is Henry. I could take that. To start, the JV will be capitalized with approximately $150 million to establish the seed portfolio. It's going to be a diversified seed portfolio, all first lien that takes into account the composition of both the JV and the remaining CCAP portfolio. The -- in terms of the future capitalization of the JV, we expect the sizing to be around $150 million to $200 million in total size going forward here. So we don't expect the size to meaningfully grow as far as the asset profile of the JV goes. It's going to be consistent with the broader CCAP portfolio focusing on first lien investments.

Finian O'Shea: So should we expect the buyback to be rather swiftly executed?

Jason Breaux: Fin, it's Jason. I think that's -- part of the objective here is to accelerate the ability to generate liquidity and deleveraging for CCAP so that we can both get leverage into our target range as well as start to capture some of the discount on the stock price through buybacks.

Henry Chung: Just to add to that, the buybacks are going to be executed through a broker under our Rule 10b5-1 plan. So the pace of the buyback is going to be subject to the plan's trading parameters as well as the applicable regulatory requirements.

And even if you were to look at the same time period on a year-over-year basis.

I will say that there's certainly a lot of early looks and early reads out there, which may indicate that the pipeline going into the end of the year, beginning of next year will be quite a bit more robust in terms of deal activity. But where we sit here today in terms of just broader activity within our core market segments has quite candidly just been a bit quieter relative to what we've seen at the beginning of the year.

Mickey Schleien: And it sounds like your expectations for next year are for things to more or less remain as is. Is that correct?

Jason Breaux: Mickey, Jason Breaux here. Look, I think that right now, as Henry said that the pipeline is pretty light. What doesn't change is the continued pressure from investors for liquidity and monetizations. And with each passing day, those pressures continue to build. So there is a fair amount of, what I would call, macro uncertainty out there that is restricting some activity at this point in time. But I think we still do believe that there will be a pickup in activity going into 2027, simply driven by really more of the concern around investors needing to see liquidity from their sponsors.

Henry Chung: I think to add to that as well -- I was going to just add, what we've observed historically is that the pipeline can turn back on relatively quickly here as well. As I indicated, there's quite a bit of early preemptive deal work going on, I would say, within the market segments that we focus on, both on the sell side, where there's early looks or reads and valuations for companies that are looking to trade. So based on that, when we think about just the backlog that is resident within the core lower middle market, there certainly is the addressable market.

I think what we're just looking for here is the volumes to actually convert in the near term.

Operator: Your final question comes from the line of Robert Dodd with Raymond James.

Robert Dodd: A lot going on. I hate to go back to the JV. But if I can, on that, is that intended to be a permanent vehicle? I mean it sounds from the way you're describing it that you're selling assets down into it primarily to release liquidity for buybacks and deleveraging. And that could obviously be done if it was kind of a static pool vehicle with a static pool CLO kind of structure. And then it would attrite away over some period of time. So I mean is this meant to be a permanent JV vehicle? Or is this a tool that may have a finite life for you?

Henry Chung: Robert, this is Henry. It's -- I would think of it as a -- this is not a static pool where we're establishing a seed portfolio and having that runoff on this JV will be reinvesting. And our expectation in the near term, we'll continue to manage it as a permanent part of the CCAP portfolio, albeit it will be -- we're expecting roughly 2% of the portfolio going forward. Longer term, we'll continue to evaluate that relative to broader origination that we're seeing across the space. But for the near term, I would not consider this a one-off static pool, and we are expecting to replenish assets into the JV as the initial seed portfolio rotates.

Robert Dodd: Got it. Got it. And on the credit, obviously, I mean, nonaccruals improved a little bit. There was a legacy asset gone there. It takes a while to turn these. Your 3s ticked up a little bit. So I mean, it sounds rather like credit is kind of stable, but not where you'd want it to be, but stable. I mean can you give us any update? And I realize, again, it doesn't change very quickly quarter-to-quarter, but on like how the restructuring or turnaround progress is going within the troubled asset pool that you have?

Henry Chung: This is Henry. I could take that. I would say that with respect to the watch list, I would agree with your observations that we are seeing stability where we sit today relative to underwriting expectations and additions to the watch list that we have seen this quarter are really due to company-specific challenges that we're seeing in certain portfolio companies as opposed to broader credit degradation as a whole across the portfolio.

With that being said, and I think this is something that we've continually been clear about here is, especially in an environment like we're in today, where portfolio turnover velocity has just been muted, given the LBO environment that we're in, I would expect that the rotation of assets, particularly those on the watch list, are just going to be longer-term exercises in terms of maximizing recovery. We're not looking to fire sale any assets just to get them off the watch list.

And as a result, we're prepared and looking to maximize long-term recoveries by taking a long-term approach to each of these assets, whether it's truly just a one-off short-term watch list inclusion or a longer-term change of control. So hopefully, that gives you some color in terms of just what we're observing to date, but our expectation here is that we'll continue to look towards maximizing longer-term recoveries with respect to the watch list.

Operator: We have one more question from Christopher Nolan with Ladenburg Thalmann.

Christopher Nolan: Given the slow LBO market and so forth, is that forcing you guys to extend the maturity of maturing investments?

Henry Chung: Thanks for the question, Chris. We've seen that become more prevalent within investments where sponsors are electing to extend duration for investments as opposed to looking to sell them today at current valuations. And what we're seeing here is that this is not necessarily indicative of companies that are in stress, but more so a determination from the sponsor's perspective that there's further value creation that can happen at the underlying portfolio companies, whether it be organically or inorganically. And as a result, they're looking for -- from support from the lenders to be able to continue to execute on their equity thesis.

Typically, how we approach these discussions is it's an opportunity for us to reprice the respective loans when those asks come across. So what you'll typically see in conjunction with an extension ask is fees or an increase in spread or both. So we take that as an opportunity to reunderwrite as well as reprice the loan to the extent that we would like to stay in the loan. And to the extent that we would not like to stay in the loan, then we elect to get taken out. So that's our approach, but we're absolutely in an environment where extension asks are certainly more commonplace than they have been several years ago.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Jason Breaux for closing remarks.

Jason Breaux: Okay. Thank you, operator. And I just wanted to say thank you to our shareholders and analysts for their interest in CCAP and all the questions, and we look forward to speaking with everyone again soon.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3164. Ford Just Proved Its EV Battery Health Barely Degrades After 5 Years

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

2021 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs have kept most of their battery and range after thousands of miles on the road.

Real-world battery life for phones, laptops and other electronic devices can diminish over years of use, but does the same happen to electric cars after thousands of miles and hundreds of recharges? According to data published by Ford this week: Yes, but not as badly as you might fear.

The automaker published a report analyzing the battery state of health of more than 36,000 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs sold to customers across the US and Canada during the initial 2021 model year. After more than five years on the road — and an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven — the fleet averaged 92% battery health.

I call that impressive, but not totally surprising. That battery durability data is largely in line with what I’ve seen reported across the industry by other automakers and independent analysts.

One of the biggest concerns of early EV adopters a decade ago (also shared by fence-sitters today) is long-term reliability. The battery is by far the most expensive component of an electric car, and owners want to know their shiny new EV will last as long as the combustion car it replaces.

Battery longevity is particularly important as more used EVs enter the market. Many experts (myself included) have touted pre-owned and off-lease EV deals as a way to bypass the electric-car price premium, but shoppers may be hesitant to roll the dice on higher-mileage vehicles. Many fear a used EV won’t meet their range needs or, worse, could blindside them with an expensive battery replacement.

Ford’s study is another data point that could help allay those worries.

Ford examined more than 36,000 individual vehicles delivered to customers across all 50 US states and Canada during the EV’s first year of sales. A little more than five years later, the automaker says that around 95% of vehicles surveyed retained between 87% and 97% of their battery health (an average of 92%) across the entire 2021 fleet after an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven.

Better battery health means an EV keeps delivering more of its advertised range as the odometer climbs. The 2021 Mustang Mach-E rolled off the assembly line with an EPA-estimated range between 211 and 305 miles, depending on the spec, which means that owners lost around 16 to 24 miles of range over time, according to my back-of-the-napkin math.

That said, there’s no beating the chemistry. Around 2,000 vehicles in the group crossed the 100,000-mile mark, retaining around 91% health. A smaller subset of about 30 drivers reached 200,000 miles in their Mach-Es, with an average battery health of 88%. More miles, it seems, means more wear.

At the extreme anecdotal end of the spectrum, one owner put more than 400,000 miles on his original battery — though Ford didn’t state the specific health of that 2022 Mach-E.

An independent study published by Aviloo earlier this year adds credence to Ford’s reported numbers. An Austrian EV battery diagnostics firm analyzed over 500,000 EVs from 20 global brands to measure battery degradation — at 50,000, 100,000 and 150,000 kilometers — finding that many popular models maintained over 90% battery health at high mileage.

Tesla’s Model Y, which competes directly with the Mach-E, was found to hold around 90.3% battery health at 150,000 kilometers (93,205 miles). Aviloo reported that the Volkswagen ID4 and Hyundai Ioniq 5 showed 90.6% and 92.8% retention, respectively, over the same surveyed mileage. The first-generation Nissan Leaf — a much older EV with a smaller battery — showed more degradation at 86.3%, an unfortunate double whammy given its shorter initial range.

According to Ford’s engineers and battery chemists, the Mach-E’s battery was designed to last at least 10 years, adding that the 2021 models in the study use an older nickel-cobalt-manganese, or NCM, chemistry.

Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle platform, which will underpin the upcoming Fathom small electric pickup, will use a newer lithium iron phosphate chemistry. That will come with unique charging needs and different battery management calibration than its Class of 2021. The UEV architecture is also built around robust bidirectional charging, so we’ll have to check back in five or so years to see how using your car to power your home affects long-term battery health.

#3162. You can change Windows settings directly from a search now – how to try it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview enhances the Search feature so that you can access specific settings right from a search window.

Microsoft has been on a kick lately trying to improve and enhance Windows 11, including sprucing up Search, which is now simpler, cleaner, and friendlier. And there’s another cool trick that Search has up its sleeve: Available in the Beta channel of the latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview, Search will give you access to specific Windows settings and commands. Known as inline actions, this latest skill is designed to help you directly complete certain tasks. That means you no longer need to know exactly where or how to find the setting you need.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

Curious about built-in features such as Dark mode, Bluetooth, screen brightness, Remote Desktop, the Windows clipboard, or Windows Update? Just type the name or phrase in the Search field. The results then display an Open button that you can select to go directly to the related setting.

“A new Windows Search experience built on WinUI 3 is beginning to roll out,” Microsoft said on a web page announcing the latest Insiders build. “It’s faster, more efficient, and features a streamlined design that makes results easier to scan. Inline actions let you quickly complete tasks directly. Turn on dark mode or Bluetooth, adjust your screen brightness, mute your device, or arrange windows from Windows Search.”

I tried this with several different Windows settings, and the results window pointed me to the right screens for tweaking them. Though I know where most Windows settings are located by now, there are still times when I forget how to reach certain ones. This new skill promises to be a time saver whenever I face that challenge.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC

Here’s another handy enhancement. How often do you type a word or term in Windows Search only to misspell it? With the latest update, Search will now better understand what you actually mean and match you with the correct results. Type “drak” instead of “dark,” for example, and you’ll still see the results for Dark mode.

Microsoft promises these latest improvements to Windows Search will continue to be fine-tuned over the next few weeks. And there’s more in the new Preview build.

Ever run into trouble using Windows Hello facial recognition in a dark area? Now, your screen will temporarily brighten up to help you sign in under those conditions. To enable this option, head to Settings, select Account, select Sign-in options, and then click Facial recognition. Turn on the switch for “Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition.”

The latest Insiders build also tweaks features such as Live captions, Gaming, File Explorer, and Microsoft 365 cloud storage.

Also: How I used ChatGPT to talk me through fixing a corrupted gaming PC

To grab this update, you’ll have to join the Windows Insiders Program if you’re not already registered. You can then sign up for the Beta or Experimental channel, either of which will give you access to the new Search skills and other features. Make sure you’re running the Beta Preview Build 26320.9876 or higher. To check, go to Settings, select System, and then click About. The Windows Info section will indicate the build number.

As for regular Windows users not enrolled in the Insiders Program, the new changes should reach you relatively soon. I’d expect them to roll out with the December Patch Tuesday update arriving on December 8, so that Microsoft can squeeze them in before the end of the year.

But recently I’ve been hands-on with the Eight Sleep Pod 6 and Orion Sleep System, two of the best smart mattresses that use active cooling to create even temperatures. As well as being the priciest upfront, the Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the only one with a mandatory subscription. Starting at $17/month, it includes sleep tracking and is essential for operating the Pod. Orion also has a sleep tracking subscription but it's optional (although more expensive at $250/year). Bear, of course, is subscription-free.

Bear blows both smart covers out of the water when it comes to benefits, offering a 365-night sleep trial and a limited lifetime warranty. Orion and Eight Sleep both offer just a 30-night trial and 2-year warranty.

The Pod 6 and Orion Sleep System both come in two parts: the cover and a control tower. The cover is fitted with water pipes, attach to the tower via tube.

In terms of design, the tower is the primary difference between the two. The Orion tower is bigger and bulkier but also has a more design-forward finish. The Eight Sleep Pod 6 is quieter, however.

The Bear Elite Hybrid is an entirely different beast. One of the best hybrid mattresses, it's made from layers of mattress springs and foams. The cover is woven with Celliant fibers to draw away heat, while a copper-infused foam layer further aids temperature control.

The Eight Sleep Pod 6 and Orion covers are designed to make minimal difference to the support and cushioning of your mattress. I tested both on the Leesa Original mattress and, overall, I think this is accurate. That means your comfort is dependent on the mattress beneath.

Dive into our Bear Elite Hybrid mattress review to learn more about the pressure relief, edge support and motion isolation of this top-rated mattress.

Both covers keep the temperature at 'snug', staying far away from 'shivering' or 'sauna'. I haven't had a sweaty 3 a.m. wake-up in months.

The Bear Elite Hybrid has a more traditional approach to cooling. (Although with its Celliant fibers and copper-infused foams, it's hardly simple.)

Despite its lack of active cooling technology, our hands-on testing showed heat didn't linger in the Bear Elite. And our thermal cam backed us up. While the Bear Elite Hybrid warmed quickly, it kicked out excess heat at an incredible pace. After just four minutes of our tester leaving the mattress, it had nearly returned to the original temperature.

While the Bear Elite Hybrid is impressive, it's not as versatile as the Eight Sleep or the Orion Sleep System. And nothing touches the Eight Sleep when it comes to quick changes — buttons on the side of the cover allow you to adjust the temperature without unlocking your phone.

Orion and Eight Sleep both offer sleep tracking alongside their advanced cooling features. For Eight Sleep, the sleep tracking is part of the mandatory subscription. For Orion, it's an optional add-on.

I've tested both alongside my Oura Ring 5, our top rated sleep tracker this year. Overall, I've been impressed with the quality and accuracy of the information. Both capture sleep stages and duration that line up with both the data from my Oura Ring and my recollection of the night.

However when it comes to the details, the Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the winner. It captures a massive amount of data and displays it in easy-to-read graphics. For the Orion, sleep tracking feels like an add-on. With Eight Sleep, it's integral.

Eight Sleep also has a smart alarm built into the the cover, which vibrates when it senses a light sleep stage. Orion preps you to wake up with gentle warmth but the Eight Sleep Pod 6 does a better job at rousing you.

✅ You experience hot flashes: The Eight Sleep's hot flash mode works to quickly counteract sudden temperature fluctuations. It should kick in while you're sleeping but you can also turn it on in the app if you feel a hot flash coming on.

✅ You want detailed sleep tracking: Eight Sleep's Autopilot delivers accurate and detailed sleep data. Plus, it puts it all into handy graphics to give you an instant picture of sleep trends and changes.

✅ You want control at the touch of a button: Simply press the button on the side of the cover to turn the heat up or down in the night. The Eight Sleep isn't a mind reader, so this allows you to tweak it to fit your needs.

✅ You want smart cooling without the expense: The Orion can match the Eight Sleep (and the Bear Elite Hybrid) when it comes to temperature control, offering active cooling at a lower price.

✅ You and your partner can never agree on the thermostat: Both the Orion and Eight Sleep allow you to set a different temperature on each side of the mattress. With the Orion, you can do so for less.

✅ You need a new bed: If you go for the Orion or Eight Sleep, you'll need to buy a new mattress as well (or stick with the one you have). The Bear Elite Hybrid doesn't just offer cooling — it's a great bed all round.

✅ You don't experience major temperature swings: If you often wake up stuffy but hot sleeping isn't ruining your night, you might not require high-tech active cooling. The Bear will keep you comfortable without the expense.

#3160. Apple’s new HomeView to add two major features not yet announced, per leaks

Apple’s HomeView arrives this Friday (pre-order here), but leaks indicate there are already two major new features in the works that haven’t been announced. Here’s what to expect.

It’s been a busy product launch season for Apple, and the company isn’t done quite yet.

Two new Home products arrive in stores this Friday, November 13: Apple HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K.

Yet despite the HomeView still being days away from launch, leaks in Apple code have already revealed two unannounced features that are in the works.

Leaker pdfu discovered evidence in HomeView 27.2 software that Apple is preparing for the product to add security camera functionality.

Based on pdfu’s findings, much of the work has already been done for HomeView to integrate with HomeKit Secure Video.

However, Apple hasn’t announced any sort of security camera functionality, so there’s clearly still more work to be done and it’s always possible the feature is never enabled.

Additionally, pdfu found a key change in iOS 27.3’s beta that reveals support for third-party AI apps is coming to HomeView.

HomeView has a unique third-party app story. There’s no App Store, but the product can run CarPlay-compatible apps from your iPhone automatically. At launch, only audio and video apps will be supported.

But iOS 27.3’s beta code adds “conversational apps” as a third category of supported apps. That’s what AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude are classified as in CarPlay.

Nobody should buy a HomeView in the hope of these two features being added. But if you are interested in HomeView, it sounds like Apple has an ambitious set of software updates planned for its new product.

#3159. Got $10,000? 3 Hot Stocks to Buy That Could Make You a Fortune

Grail, Agility Robotics, and Sandisk could deliver multibagger gains in the future.

It might not seem like the best time to invest in high-growth stocks. Elevated Treasury yields are still weighing down stocks, and the market is digesting the impact of the midterm elections -- in which the Democrats took over the House, Senate, and several governorships.

But if you can look past those near-term challenges, you'll find plenty of promising growth stocks that could deliver massive gains for investors who can stomach a little volatility. Let's see why three of those growth stocks -- Grail (GRAL -2.61%), Agility Robotics (AGLT +4.56%), and Sandisk (SNDK -2.99%) -- could be a great place to lock up a fresh $10,000 investment.

Grail develops Galleri, a blood test designed to detect dozens of cancers before any symptoms appear. The FDA hasn't approved Galleri yet, but Grail sells it on a cash-only basis to affluent customers, certain businesses, and hospital pilot programs for about $949 per test.

Through those cash sales, Grail's revenue rose from $93 million in 2023 to $147 million in 2025. But by 2028, analysts expect its revenue to reach $275 million as an FDA approval expands its market to include private insurance and Medicare plans. In late September, the FDA endorsed a premarket approval for Galleri based on its safety, efficacy, and potential benefits. Those endorsements are non-binding, but they suggest it could be fully approved in the near future.

With a market cap of $5.8 billion, Grail isn't cheap at 34 times this year's sales. But if the FDA fully approves its blood test, it could grow much larger as it's adopted by more hospitals. That's why its stock still has more upside potential -- even after its 44% year-to-date gain.

Agility Robotics, a developer of humanoid robots for warehouses, logistics hubs, and manufacturing plants, went public through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) on Nov. 4. Its stock opened at $11.38 per share on Nov. 5, but it's pulled back to about $9 as of this writing. However, it could have plenty of room to grow.

Agility's flagship robot, Digit, can move heavy items and navigate aisles, stairs, and ramps on its own. Its top investors include Nvidia and Amazon. Its growing list of enterprise customers includes Toyota, GXO Logistics, MercadoLibre, and Schaffer.

Agility only generated $1.8 million in revenue in 2025, and it hasn't deployed its first Digit v5 robots yet. However, it has a backlog of over $300 million. Agility believes it can deploy its first Digit v5 robots by the end of 2026, and accelerate its annual deployments to 800 units in 2027, 7,000 units in 2030, and up to 25,000 units in 2035. To keep those robots running, its customers will need to pay recurring "robot as a service" (RaaS) subscription fees.

With a market cap of $489 million, Agility might seem expensive relative to its near-term revenue growth. But at its estimated $8,500 monthly RaaS rate, it could generate $2.55 billion in annual revenue from 25,000 deployed robots. That's why Agility's stock could deliver multibagger gains over the next few years as economies of scale kick in.

Sandisk, which was spun off from Western Digital in early 2025, is one of the world's largest producers of NAND (flash) memory chips. Its stock has declined 64% after hitting a record high of $2,335 on June 25, but that pullback could be a golden buying opportunity.

Sandisk is usually considered a cyclical stock that follows the memory market's boom-and-bust cycles. But as the AI market expanded over the past few years, Sandisk launched ultra-dense enterprise solid-state drives (SSDs) that consolidated dozens of hardware server racks onto single drives. These SSDs are also smaller, faster, more power-efficient, and less prone to physical damage than platter-based hard disk drives (HDDs).

In fiscal 2026 (which ended this July), Sandisk's revenue surged 176% as it turned profitable. From fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2029, analysts expect its revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 44% and 62%, respectively. It looks ridiculously cheap at 4 times this year's earnings -- because it's still valued as a cyclical stock -- but it could command a much higher valuation if the AI market's acceleration continues to boost its enterprise SSD sales.

#3158. NASA Just Made a Bunch of Moon Base Announcements: Here’s What They Are

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The agency just unveiled new lunar missions, a nuclear-powered rover and $10 billion in contracts to build a moon base for astronauts.

NASA just wrapped up its Max Power event, the agency’s first-ever aerospace technology expo that took place Wednesday through Sunday at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Featuring discussions, panels, announcements and technology demonstrations, the biggest part of the event was NASA’s update on the Ignition initiative, which promises to put a base on the moon by 2032.

The Moon Base Program is an expensive endeavor that requires the help of various space companies to complete on time. Max Power discussed the various technologies and projects to make a base work, including the new CLPS 2 contract, a nuclear-powered moon rover and other lunar architecture.

NASA will rely heavily on commercial aerospace companies for many of these components: Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, SpaceX, Voyager Technologies and ispace-US. Most of those companies have also been supplying tech for the Artemis program, which is slated to launch its third mission in 2027 and send people back to the moon in 2028. While the Artemis missions are important in their own right, NASA is also using them as a precursor to the Moon Base. That’s one of many reasons why it was a huge deal when Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket exploded in May.

“We are building the moon base mission by mission,” NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said during Max Power. “When our astronauts return to the moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the moon base already waiting for them on the surface.”

The CLPS 2 contract is part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative, which plays a pivotal role in the moon base’s construction. The goal is to send materials and equipment to the moon ahead of time, so humans can immediately start building the base when they arrive.

The CLPS 2 contract builds on the CLPS 1.0 contract to develop the infrastructure and vehicles, including cargo landers, necessary to continuously ferry supplies and crew between Earth and the lunar surface. To fund these efforts, NASA paired the $10 billion CLPS 2 budget with an expanded CLPS 1.0 budget, which increased from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion.

The cargo landers get cargo from space to the moon’s surface, but they also have to be transported there. NASA announced $1.3 billion in funding to Blue Origin, Arrow Science and Technology and Impulse Space to perform this step. They’ll make Orbital Transfer Vehicles, or OTVs, that act like “long-distance freight trucks” to carry the cargo landers and eventually deploy them safely to the moon’s surface.

In addition to building the vehicles that do this, NASA says three missions are slated for completion. First, research must assess how to reduce human risk and determine the best ways to deploy the CLPS landers. Second, NASA’s MoonFall drones will assess the moon and find the most optimal spot for a base. The third mission is to test the infrastructure to ensure it works as designed.

NASA took some time to talk about Promise, also known as Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping and In-Situ Exploration, an important vehicle for early moon exploration. The agency awarded Blue Origin a $94 million development contract, plus a performance-based $140 million for lunar delivery. Once deployed, the nuclear-powered rover will be managed by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory at Caltech, which oversees NASA’s other rovers, NASA’s Deep Space Network and the Voyager probes.

Unlike solar-powered rovers, Promise’s nuclear core allows it to operate continuously through two-week lunar nights and in permanently shadowed regions where the sun never reaches. Its goal is to analyze regolith, hunt for ice and conduct general exploration.

While most of NASA’s recent announcements focused on getting hardware to the moon, the final segment laid the groundwork for surface infrastructure, specifically, long-term habitability so astronauts can actually be there.

To power this presence, NASA awarded contracts for energy storage and transmission to Honeybee Robotics (a Blue Origin company) and Yank Technologies. Their solar arrays, batteries and wireless power hardware will culminate in the Mini-Communications and Solar Tower (miniCast), assembled at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, before being deployed to the moon.

NASA is also trying to tackle the myriad problems that must be solved for a moon base to succeed. One of the initiatives announced at Max Power is the Moon Base Student Challenge, which asks students to help build humanity’s future on the moon, with $1 million in prizes for winners with the best ideas.

“We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world,” Isaacman said during his speech, which was packed with students and kids, according to Space.com.

#3157. Can you still trust Proton?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The company’s reputation took a major hit two weeks ago, when 404 Media published a detailed report, based on leaked Slack messages and interviews with anonymous insiders. The story detailed a push by Proton CEO Andy Yen to — in his own words — “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity.”

Also: Is your browser’s free VPN enough? I tested 4 against Proton VPN

After one employee proposed spending at least a few days on penetration testing before shipping new code, Yen reportedly said, “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure. Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” According to 404 Media’s account, Yen’s message for Proton engineers was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

After the original story broke, 404 Media posted a follow-up story reporting that the company had canceled its “re-interviews” that were intended to assess how developers were adopting AI. A 404 Media podcast was titled “Proton’s CEO Is Putting AI Before Security.”

Reddit has an especially active Proton community with 345,000 weekly visitors. It quickly filled up with so many comments — the majority of them negative — that moderators created a single megathread to help keep track of the different threads, including pages for general criticism, support of the AI usage, and “leaving your goodbyes.”

Also: Best VPN services 2026: Expert tested and recommended

Given the level of interest, it’s not surprising that Yen chose that forum to post a public message to the community. In it, he apologized for “hurtful” remarks, adding that he’s “determined to do better.”

He also addressed the topic of AI-based security reviews:

But most importantly, I need to categorically state that our use of AI will never be at the expense of security. In the past year, contrary to what has been alleged, actually additional layers of security review have been added to meet the threat posed by hostile AIs scanning Proton’s open source code for vulnerabilities. Fast and secure need not be mutually exclusive. We also leverage AI to find vulnerabilities in our own code before attackers do. Our code is open source, and its security remains open for all to verify. [emphasis in original]

Nothing in the 404 Media reporting demonstrates that Proton weakened its encryption or shipped insecure code because of AI. The damage is different: Yen’s remarks undermined confidence that management will consistently respect the security processes its customers rely on.

In a blog post that Proton shared with ZDNET ahead of its publication today, the company followed up on Yen’s promise to “lift the hood on how we use AI internally at Proton.” The post, titled “How Proton keeps your data secure in the age of AI,” was signed by the Proton Team and emphasizes Proton’s secure architecture, with end-to-end, zero-access encryption:

We do not hold the keys to your emails, files, or passwords, so we cannot read them, and no AI tool can, either. Our documented security governance policies have not changed since June 2024, before AI was even a major factor in our work here, and they all still apply.

On Reddit, Yen said, “AI is here, and it will unquestionably change how software is developed forever, and Proton must also change.” Today’s post clarified that code receives the same checks whether it is written by a human, by an AI agent, or by a combination of both. Every change receives automated security scans but also requires human approval; sensitive changes, such as core cryptography work, require review by specialist teams. Major feature designs are also reviewed for security, dependencies, testing, and deployment plans.

Also: I can access my home PCs remotely for free – no VPN needed

Those policies address the most serious technical concerns raised by the current controversy, although outsiders have no way to know from the policy alone how consistently those safeguards are followed in day-to-day development.

Should a modern software company use AI for security? Proton argues that it can’t afford not to.

Because of AI, attacks that once might have required a nation-state can now be executed by almost anyone. A defender relying on manual processes and hand-crafted tools is bringing a knife to a gunfight. An attacker only needs to find one flaw, while a defender needs to close all of them. AI is the only tool that makes that defense possible. Cybersecurity is an arms race, and the teams working on security at Proton have been some of the earliest adopters of AI, because the safety of your data depends on winning that race.

But that argument doesn’t really address the objection. The current controversy isn’t about whether Proton should use AI to find vulnerabilities; it’s about whether pressure for “AI velocity” can override the judgment of engineers responsible for keeping its products secure.

Proton says it uses AI to review code changes, identify vulnerabilities through continuous security reviews, and monitor an attack surface that has “grown far beyond what unaided humans could monitor.” The company uses its own models alongside non-public cyber models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

The modern software development landscape is torn by two opposing forces. On one side, you have AI-based tools that are routinely finding nightmarish vulnerabilities in existing codebases and then exploiting them immediately. On the other side, you have a global movement that’s skeptical of the benefits of AI and outright opposed to construction of the data centers where they run.

Much of Proton’s growth over the past few years has been the direct result of people trying to escape big tech. So it shouldn’t be a surprise that many of Proton’s customers — at least those who are passionate enough to visit a Reddit forum — are deeply skeptical of anything related to AI.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

In a traditional software company, that realization would have led management to cautiously roll out AI-based features and reveal its AI-centric security strategy more deliberately. That didn’t happen here, obviously. Those blunt remarks from the CEO exposed a management culture that many employees and customers found troubling. It’s difficult to restore trust, both within the workforce and among customers, after that kind of public display of contempt.

Ironically, one of Yen’s comments from the original 404 Media story describes the company’s current dilemma with devastating accuracy.

In a Slack message, Yen told a Proton engineer, “perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.” The implication was that he was urging the employee to lie, or at least shade the truth. In fact, as Yen himself told a random Reddit commenter:

I do not believe perception should be more important than truth. I am stating that unfortunately it often ends up being the case. If you place it into the context in which it was said, it can be understood as, “it doesn’t matter that the truth is that Proton’s PQC implementation is better, this truth is irrelevant as long as it is not perceived to be this way, and we therefore need to correct that perception”

That’s Proton’s challenge now, distilled to its essence. It takes seconds to destroy a reputation. It can take months or years to recover from the perception that the company and its management can no longer be trusted.

Personally, I will continue to use Proton Pass and Proton VPN, both of which are solid, reliable products. But I’ve moved my secondary email accounts (which I had migrated from Gmail to Proton Mail); they’re now running on Fastmail. I had been considering making the switch for a long time, primarily because Proton Mail’s performance has been too slow for my taste. Current events just hastened that switch.

#3155. I tested the Google Pixel Tag and it’s the most findable tracker for Android phones — plus it does something Apple AirTag can't

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Pixel Tag delivers an outstanding tracking experience for Android users, matching the AirTag’s $29 price point while beating it out with superior Precision Finding range and persistent alerts when the batter level gets low.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Over the past few years, I’ve tested my fair share of Bluetooth trackers — ranging from wallet-thin cards like the Statik SmartCard Incognito to the Pebblebee Halo, which can potentially help elderly individuals in emergency situations. Google has expanded its Find Hub network, finally giving Android users plenty of options, but many of these trackers share one glaring limitation: pinpoint proximity tracking.

While iPhone users have long enjoyed the superb performance of Precision Finding — leaning on Ultra Wideband (UWB) for pinpoint accuracy — most Android trackers don’t have that luxury. Instead, they rely on basic Bluetooth proximity that only shows broad geographic circles on a map.

Google’s Pixel Tag is one of the few Android trackers that packages Ultra Wideband (UWB) and Bluetooth Channel Sounding directly into Google’s native ecosystem. As a result, the Pixel Tag delivers true visual Precision Finding to Android devices. After putting it to the test, I found it holds one distinct advantage over the AirTag and one of the best Bluetooth trackers you can get.

Ultra-Wideband (UWB) + Bluetooth Channel Sounding

Easily the best feature of the Pixel Tag is its ability to lock down an exact position with outstanding Precision Finding range, which actually managed to outperform even Apple's AirTag 2 in my testing. Using the Find My Device app on an Android phone, you get intuitive on-screen visual guidance, complete with compass-like directional arrows and real-time distance readouts that point you right where you need to go.

While the AirTag 2 tapped out around 74 feet in my testing before dropping its Ultra Wideband connection, the Pixel Tag held on slightly farther, reaching roughly 82 feet. That extra reach eliminates the guesswork of tracking down misplaced gear, like my keys when I've completely forgotten where I left them. Plus, you can still trigger a loud audio chime if the tag slips deep between couch cushions and you can't spot it right away.

The AirTag has an unmistakable look, but Google has delivered an equally compelling design — especially when it comes to size. At just 5.4mm thick, the Pixel Tag is significantly sleeker than the AirTag, making it far less conspicuous when slipped into a standard wallet. With its minimalist, matte-finished polycarbonate body, I really dig the pebble-like aesthetic, which does a far better job of masking smudges and fingerprints than the AirTag's scratch-prone stainless steel back.

Even with that slimmed-down profile, Google didn’t cut corners on durability, outfitting it with a rugged IP67 dust- and water-resistance rating. Plus, swapping out the CR2032 coin-cell battery is painless — all it takes is a quick twist of the back cover.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Beyond tracking down my keys, wallet, backpack, or other gear, the Pixel Tag offers another standout feature you won’t find on the AirTag: the ability to ring your phone. With a simple double-press of the physical button on the front, you can instantly trigger your phone to ring at full volume — even if it's set to silent or vibrate. This reverse-finding capability is a lifesaver in a crunch when you're rushing out the door and can't find your phone anywhere.

One of the biggest annoyances I have with the AirTag is discovering weeks or even months later that it's dead. Sure, my iPhone might have sent a low-battery notification, but those alerts are easy to forget. That’s why I’m stoked about the Pixel Tag’s persistent automated reminders, which offer huge peace of mind if I overlook that initial heads-up.

Google rates the user-replaceable CR2032 coin-cell battery for up to a full year of typical use. While I haven’t had the Pixel Tag long enough to drain it down and trigger an alert firsthand, knowing Find Hub will send a notification “every 2 weeks until it’s replaced” ensures it won't quietly drop off my radar. Usually, I’m not a fan of that level of notification nagging, but in this case, it's a welcome safety net.

Despite having some key advantages over the AirTag, there’s one area where the Pixel Tag falls behind its rival: accessory availability. You can find an AirTag mount, leather loop, rugged clip, or pet collar attachment with a quick search online. The Pixel Tag, however, launches with very few options.

In fact, Google doesn't even offer any official accessories right out of the gate. The only ones I’ve been able to track down so far are basic silicone cases from Walmart. Because the Pixel Tag’s design doesn't include a built-in lanyard hole or keyring cutout, you'll need a dedicated case or adhesive mount just to attach it to your keys or backpack. For early adopters, finding the exact style or mount you want right now will require some patience while third-party makers ramp up production.

Considering how long the Pixel line has been around, you’d think Google would’ve come out with its own AirTag rival sooner. Even so, the Pixel Tag is a long-overdue addition — and it’s easily one of the most capable and well-rounded Bluetooth trackers on the market.

Between its class-leading Precision Finding range, compact design, and reverse-phone-ringing feature, it addresses the pinpoint tracking compromises that have long plagued the Android ecosystem. The only other real alternatives with Ultra Wideband support are Motorola’s Moto Tag and Samsung’s SmartTag3. You still get all the essential safeguards expected from a flagship tracker, too, including left-behind alerts and a dedicated Lost Mode that allows anyone who finds your gear to scan it and get in touch.

At $29 for a single one (or $99 for a four-pack), Google matches Apple dollar for dollar — but delivers greater range and features the AirTag simply can’t match.

Ring's $250 flying indoor security camera is set to arrive in January. We got a first look at the Drone Cam in action.

Ring Home Security has taken flight, and the brand’s tiny new home security drone is less expensive than we thought. The Ring Drone Cam, a $250 mini indoor drone camera, was announced on Tuesday as part of the brand’s new arm, Ring Robotics. It uses a learned map of your home to zoom around autonomously for up to 8 minutes at a time with custom routes to record places a couple of fixed cameras can’t.

The small drone weighs just 5.8 ounces and houses a pair of 2K-resolution cameras mounted on the front and bottom, respectively. The cameras use bright LED lights to enable day or night monitoring, sending a live feed or recorded video to your device. The LEDs are also meant to ward off potential intruders peering in from the outside.

You can program the flying cam to make regular flights or send it on specific missions to check on the dog or see if the stove was left on. The Drone Cam also syncs with other Ring cameras and sensors to respond automatically when windows and doors open at certain hours.

If you’re thinking, “Wait, didn’t Ring already launch a drone camera?” you’d be right — sort of. The brand “launched” the Ring Always Home Cam in 2020. The $250 indoor drone had a limited, invitation-only release but was never available for public sale. We’ve been assured this latest iteration is ready for prime time, though it’s still not available for preorder on Amazon.

Ring founder and CEO Jamie Siminoff demoed the drone, which has been in development for more than five years, in an event space set up to replicate a home. During the demo, the small drone lifted gently from the dock and rose to about eye level, where it hovered as if to say “hello” to the group of journalists gathered around.

Once airborne, the drone turned toward the adjacent room and whirred off to investigate. After a few seconds of scanning, the drone returned to the first room, docked and resumed charging.

While in flight, the Ring Drone Cam made a notably loud buzz reminiscent of a golf cart in reverse. Siminoff quickly noted that the sound was intentional, meant to deter potential intruders and alert home dwellers to the drone’s presence.

The 1-minute flight was enough to cover two medium-sized rooms, though the drone can fly up to eight minutes on a full charge before needing about an hour to recharge. Ring reps told me it can monitor a home up to 3,500 square feet – more than enough for most – but Siminoff says it plans to improve the range over time.

If you’re worried about the drone knocking over vases and flying into ceiling fans like I was, Siminoff assured us the preprogrammed coverage zone is tight.

The drone is powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the device’s cameras, specialized vision models, sensors and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” (We’ll see for ourselves once we get a unit in for testing.)

To create your drone’s fly zone, you carry it through the space where it intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points like doors, windows or a nursery. You can add rooms and areas based on your home’s layout and security preferences.

The $250 Ring Drone Cam isn’t yet available for preorder, but Ring representatives at the launch event assured us it will be soon, and units are set to begin shipping in late January 2027. We’ll update this story when it becomes available for preorder or purchase.

#3152. How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain – and what you can do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New research provides a stark look at the AI supply chain and the risks it brings to businesses.

Artificial intelligence companies worldwide are bringing a new wave of vulnerabilities and security issues to the digital supply chain, researchers warn.

According to a new report published by Black Kite on Tuesday, there now exists a “widespread cybersecurity weakness” across the “rapidly expanding ecosystem of companies developing, deploying, and supporting artificial intelligence.”

AI and smart solutions don’t automatically equate with safe solutions. In a study titled “2026 AI Supply Chain Report: The Risks Behind Your AI Relationships,” Black Kite says that many AI suppliers — the companies that develop and deploy AI services to today’s businesses — are struggling with “basic security practices.”

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

According to the research, after examining the companies themselves, along with their software, integrations, and components, researchers found failures to patch critical vulnerabilities, protect credentials, authenticate users and email, and address network security issues.

The study analyzes 18,160 AI companies worldwide, ranging from 0-10 employees to more than 1,000 employees. A company’s AI involvement was determined through reviews of company products and services and primary business activities, covering six broad groups: everyday application development; AI development and implementation; AI applications in specialized sectors such as healthcare, IT, and finance; industrial organizations; and AI foundations working on data, compute, and modeling.

A small percentage of assessed companies are considered “unclassified,” and the study excluded businesses that use AI only incidentally.

In addition, unusual network activity was detected at 44.3% of organizations, and botnet-related activity was recorded at 41.8% of AI companies.

AI’s main business appeal is its ability to integrate with existing software and platforms to handle manual tasks, heavy lifting, and tedious, time-consuming work, freeing employees to focus on work that requires human oversight.

Enterprises are investing billions of dollars in AI. Menlo’s 2026 research estimates that enterprise AI spend reached $37 billion in 2025, with half of overall spend going to AI apps. In total, 76% of enterprise AI solutions are purchased rather than built internally.

However, the moment an AI or automated component is introduced into a corporate ecosystem or operational platform, any security problems it has impact the user — and each additional integration, such as software components or open-source tooling, may also increase the attack surface.

In an accompanying analysis of AI firms’ use of Model Context Protocol (MCP) components, which can link AI apps to business systems, 48.8% of 1,732 logged security findings were rated High or Critical, including code and command injection vulnerabilities.

Also: The new enterprise AI expert every company needs

It’s not just the AI application itself. As noted by Black Kite, AI suppliers often have access to customer data, developer environments, business infrastructure, and enterprise platforms. If the supplier’s credentials are stolen, this could expose its customers to a range of cyberattacks.

The researchers found, for example, that 19.9% of AI companies offering solutions for enterprise AI deployment had corporate login information in infostealer records, and that stolen corporate logins, overall, were linked to 6.8% of AI suppliers in the study.

Visibility matters, too, for businesses that should be monitoring their digital supply chains. However, 33.2% of AI companies assessed have a “limited” digital footprint, including their domains, subdomains, and IP addresses.

The same principles for protecting the digital supply chain apply to AI suppliers, where continual monitoring and assessment are among the best protections businesses have.

Staying informed and aware of the risks to your own business makes all the difference. As recommended by Black Kite, it takes more than a single point-in-time security assessment — frequent monitoring and engaging with suppliers to understand their technologies and dependencies can reveal potential security issues.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance?

If you find weaknesses, manage them by priority, handling ransomware-related exposures and vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild first.

Also audit an AI tool’s integrations and components, access, what data it can reach, and the potential impact of exploitation. Once you’re armed with this information, it’s possible to weigh risk and reward — and whether the AI tool is worth the potential attack exposure it brings. If you decide to keep it, limit its permissions and access to what it requires.
