It's taken a lot of work to get to this point, and my sincere hope is that we will all look back on today's call as an inflection point for the company. On today's call, after my overview, we'll begin with Jim's review of our commercial progress for Symvess.

As you know, Jim was appointed as our Chief Commercial Officer in May, and he's already making a considerable and demonstrable impact on the execution of our commercial strategy. I'll then review progress across our development programs before turning it over to Dale for a review of our financial results for the third quarter. We'll then be happy to open up the call and take your questions. Let's begin.

As we've mentioned previously, our focus for 2026 has been on advancing 3 main goals: transforming and advancing our commercial programs for Symvess, preparation and submission of our supplemental Biologics License Application, or sBLA with the FDA for our ATEV product in the dialysis access indication and commencement of a human study of our coronary tissue engineered vessels or CTEVs, in coronary artery bypass grafting. I'm pleased to report that we've made substantial progress on all 3 of these goals. Commercial adoption of Symvess accelerated during the third quarter, with sales increasing 151% over the second quarter to slightly over $1 million. Our supplemental Biologics License Application, or sBLA, is on track for submission later this month.

And we're pleased to announce that we have initiated our first human Phase IIa clinical study of CTEV in coronary artery bypass grafting, or CABG, and we are now open and screening patients. I'll now turn the call over to Jim for his review of our commercial results before I recap the progress on our pipeline programs.

Jim Mercadante: Thank you, Laura, and good morning, everyone. It's a pleasure to be speaking with all of you. As I mentioned on the last call, when I joined Humacyte, my immediate focus was to rebuild and reinvigorate our commercial effort for Symvess. I was captivated by the potential to capture meaningful market share in an area where patient outcomes can improve materially. At a baseline level, our revitalized program was designed to drive adoption of the products by hospitals, expand utilization of Symvess and establish a path to sustained growth for Symvess. To accomplish this, we completely remodeled the commercial team with a focus on ensuring our professionals had critical long-term relationships in the vascular surgery space.

Our team is already demonstrating the impact of deep industry relationships and the trust they have built across the market. We also refined our introductory pricing and incentive programs and approach to peer-to-peer professional education and our focus on hospital adoption. These initiatives were designed to ensure each element work together to help create a scalable engine that converts interest in our first-in-class product into approvals, utilization and ultimately sustained revenue growth. I am pleased to report that during our third quarter, the result of this approach is absolutely delivering immediate impact. As Laura mentioned, Symvess sales revenue for the period was $1 million.

Our revenue more than doubled from the second quarter, and we achieved our internal goal that we set for the quarter. Hospital adoption also expanded significantly with the number of hospitals ordering Symvess increasing by 44% from 34 hospitals at the end of the second quarter to 49 hospitals at the end of September 30. For those of you that understand the challenges of becoming approved as a new provider to a hospital, you can appreciate how excited we are about these results.

As momentum has continued into fourth quarter, with October sales now reaching $800,000, with the current levels of hospital adoptions and physician agreement, we are seeing and expect fourth quarter sales to at least double our Q3 results. By the end of the year, we anticipate at least 20 new hospitals to order through our network. Our strategy is delivering results. Our commercial momentum is building, and we believe Symvess is now well positioned to continue accelerating adoption and driving meaningful sustainable growth. Like Laura, I am incredibly excited about the outlook for our business. With that, I will turn it back to Laura to review our pipeline.

Laura Niklason: Thank you, Jim. So I'll start with ATEV and dialysis access. Following discussions with the FDA, our plan is to file a supplemental BLA for the ATEV in dialysis access later this month. This sBLA will be supported by results from 3 Phase III clinical studies. Publication of the V007 Phase III results in the Lancet Digital Health was very recent in the last few months. And we also recently presented the results of our V012 Phase III study in a late-breaking session at the American Society of Nephrology Kidney Week just a few weeks ago. These presentations have given the vascular surgery and nephrology communities an overview of the data that form the basis of our BLA filing.

The Phase III results on V012 were presented by Prabir Roy-Chaudhury of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and also a former President of the ASN. In the V012 Phase III trial, women on dialysis treated with the ATEV achieved functional access and use for dialysis more than 3 months sooner and spent significantly more time free of dialysis catheters over the first year than did women who received an AV fistula, which is the current standard of care for hemodialysis access.

These results also support our belief that the ATEV could represent the first major advance in dialysis access in decades, offering surgeons and patients an alternative option for patients whose risk factors for AV fistula maturation make AV fistula maturation more difficult. As many of you know, we appointed Dr. Prabir Roy-Chaudhury and Dr. Robert Kossmann as advisers to Humacyte. These are leading nephrologists who will help us prepare for the planned commercialization of the ATEV in dialysis access after it's approved by the FDA. They will also contribute to the development of health economic, reimbursement and market access strategies as well as provide important peer-to-peer scientific support, as they already have, and medical education.

Let me turn next to another meaningful opportunity for Humacyte, the CTEV in coronary artery bypass grafting or CABG. The FDA accepted our investigational new drug application for a first-in-human clinical study of the CTEV in CABG. And we initiated a Phase IIa study of the CTEV in CABG patients this month. Also, just this past weekend, 3 scientific presentations related to CTEV were made at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions Medical Conference. John Alexander, Professor of Medicine and Cardiology at the Duke Clinical Research Institute and Alan Kypson, a cardiothoracic surgeon from UNC Rex Hospital, presented an overview of the Phase IIa clinical trial protocol for our study.

And researchers from Humacyte also presented preclinical results supporting the progression of the CTEV into the first-in-human study based on extensive large animal results and work. No new off-the-shelf conduits have been introduced for study in CABG in the U.S. in the past 40 years. And our preclinical results suggest that CTEV may be a promising off-the-shelf alternative to saphenous vein grafts. To support this study, we've already completed the first large-scale manufacturing lot of our CTEV product in our commercial scale manufacturing facilities. And with that, it's my pleasure to hand the call over to Dale now for a review of our third quarter financial results. Dale?

Dale Sander: Thank you, Laura. Commercial sales of Symvess increased to $1 million for the third quarter of 2026 compared to $0.4 million in the second quarter of 2026 and $0.7 million in the third quarter of 2025. Sequential quarter sales growth and growth compared to the prior year quarter resulted from the commercialization initiatives implemented during the first half of 2026 that Jim described and an increase in the number of hospitals ordering Symvess during the most recent quarter. For the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, commercial sales of Symvess were $1.9 million compared to $1 million for the 9 months ended September 30, 2025.

Contract revenue was minimal during the third quarters of 2026 and 2025 and for the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, due to the completion of a research project and was $0.6 million for the 9 months ended September 30, 2025. Cost of goods sold was $1.4 million for the third quarter of 2026 compared to $0.3 million for the third quarter of 2025. In the third quarter of 2026, $0.6 million of cost of goods sold related to the cost of units recorded as sales revenue during the period and $0.8 million was primarily comprised of overhead related to unused production capacity.

Cost of goods sold was $4.7 million for the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, compared to $0.6 million for the 9 months ended September 30, 2025. In the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, $1.2 million of cost of goods sold related to the cost of units recorded as sales revenue during the period, $2.3 million related to inventory reserves and $1.2 million was primarily comprised of overhead related to unused production capacity. Research and development expenses were $14.1 million and $51.7 million for the 3 and 9 months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, compared to $17.3 million and $54.7 million for the same periods in 2025.

The decrease in research and development expenses during the third quarter of 2026 and during the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, compared to the prior year periods was primarily due to a reduction in noncommercial manufacturing runs and the wind down of certain programs. Research and development expenses have declined sequentially each quarter in 2026 and the $14.1 million incurred in the third quarter of 2026 was $4 million less than the $18.1 million incurred in the second quarter of 2026. General and administrative expenses were $9.0 million and $25.0 million for the 3 and 9 months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, compared to $7.6 million and $23.6 million for the same periods in 2025.

The current year increase in general and administrative expenses was primarily related to $0.6 million in net expense related to a reserve for settlement of shareholder litigation and legal costs related to the litigation. Other net income was $8.0 million and $9.5 million for the 3 and 9 months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, compared to other net income of $6.9 million and $61.3 million for the same periods in 2025. Other net income for all periods resulted primarily from the noncash remeasurement of the contingent earn-out liability and other derivative liabilities.

Net loss was $15.5 million and $70.0 million for the 3 and 9 months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, compared to a net loss of $17.5 million and $16.0 million for the same periods in 2025. The decrease in net loss for the third quarter of 2026 was primarily related to the decrease in research and development expenses. The increase in net loss for the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, was primarily due to the noncash remeasurement of the contingent earn-out liability described earlier. We had cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash of $64.9 million as of September 30, 2026.

During the quarter, the cost reduction measures that we put in place earlier in the year certainly flowed through and our net cash used in operations has declined substantially. Total net cash used in operating activities was $15.0 million and $62.1 million for the 3 and 9 months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, compared to $23.9 million and $78.9 million for the same periods in 2025. Cash used in operations decreased in '26, primarily due to lower inventory production costs and the cost reduction measures that were put in place earlier this year. With that, I will turn the call back to Laura.

Laura Niklason: Thank you, Dale. So we're very pleased with our progress that we've made this past quarter and with our remodeled commercial team and our excellent progress in our pipeline programs. With our outstanding and dedicated team, we remain committed to delivering truly transformative regenerative medicine solutions that improve patient outcomes and save limbs and save lives. We are positioned for growth and value generation for the balance of 2026 and beyond. I want to thank you for your interest in Humacyte. And operator, we're now ready to take questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Ryan Zimmerman with [ U.S. Bancorp ] BTIG.

Ryan Zimmerman: Congrats on all the progress. It's exciting to see the momentum, Laura, Dale and Jim. Maybe for Jim, just to understand more about kind of what you've changed, how you think about the durability of adoption this quarter, particularly with all these new sites. You mentioned a little bit about incentive pricing, I think, to get hospitals on board. Maybe you could just give us some more color on some of these dynamics, Jim. I think that would be very helpful.

Jim Mercadante: Sure. Happy to do so, and thanks for the question. First and foremost, I think one of the biggest impact we had, we're hiring the right leadership team and specifically those that have those vascular surgery experiences and relationships across the United States. That was one key element that we executed on all throughout Q2 that impacted and into Q3 that impacted Q3 and now impacting Q4. That's first. The second is we did redevelop and retool our marketing, our messaging and our training at the same time.

Again, doing this all throughout Q2 and partially Q3 and as it relates to pricing, it's no question that sometimes you have to -- when you're launching a particular health care system and they want to try out the product and of course, outcomes and patient care is of utmost, you want to give some type of introductory price before you get them going and get them started. So I think the combination of all that has allowed us to take off commercially. And you can see that not only in Q3, but you see that with the takeoff in Q4, as I said a little earlier, we expect to double from Q3 to Q4, continuing that trend.

So we're very excited about the progress we made. The progress will continue. And I think there's no question in our mind, we've got the right product. Now we have the right people and programs in place to get this off commercially. I hope that answers your question.

Ryan Zimmerman: Very helpful. And Laura, just turning to you on the pipeline. You're a couple of weeks away here of getting that supplemental BLA. How are you feeling about dialysis access as an approved indication? Can you give us a sense for timing of when you expect we should think about commercial activity beginning? And just any other thoughts around the build-out of the dialysis access program from a commercial perspective?

Laura Niklason: Yes. Well, on the commercial part of that question, I might toss it back over to Jim. But in general, the sBLA is coming together very well. As I mentioned on the call, we have 3 Phase III trials supporting this indication. Our target indication, not yet approved, of course, but our target indication will be in all women and in men who have certain risk factors for fistula nonmaturation. I can tell you that looking at our clinical trial data across Phase III trials, our outcomes in women are remarkably consistent and remarkably good. And this is some really strong data, and I am so pleased to be submitting this package.

So the package will go in sometime in November. And then the FDA has 30 -- I'm sorry, 60 days to accept the filing. So we expect to get BLA acceptance sometime in January, which we would, of course, announce. At that time, we'll learn about whether or not we're getting a priority review. We believe that we deserve a priority review because we have an RMAT designation for the product. However, we'll learn that in January. If we do get priority review, then that would mean we could have a PDUFA date sometime in May and then a commercial launch soon thereafter, perhaps in June.

If we do not get priority review from the FDA, then that would push our PDUFA date into September, and we would launch after that. So those are sort of the -- that's the sort of the binary question there. With respect to commercial readiness, we've already built out a budget impact model. Given that our patient populations who most benefit from ATEV in dialysis has been pretty clear from the data that's allowed us to build out a budget impact model.

And we're in the process of combining that now with Medicare closed claims data from the fee-for-service database to really understand how our vessel could impact both cost of access care and total cost of care, which CMS is very focused on for our target populations in dialysis. So all of that thinking work is well underway. And as far as the other sort of commercial approach, I'll let Jim speak to that.

Jim Mercadante: Sure, Laura. And thanks for going through that. I can tell you that just when you think about the dialysis launch, we're more than excited about it. As we are planning for this particular launch, and as Laura said, we have to figure out the actual launch date. But behind the scenes, we're actively planning our marketing campaigns and so many other things that we'll do on a commercial launch. What we get excited about are a couple of things. One, if you know dialysis and you know that market size, it's about 500,000 patients in the U.S. and about 100,000 patients enter into dialysis every year, maybe another 20,000 revisions.

So when you start to calculate a total available market for dialysis, again, this is total available market now. You're looking at a $2 billion to $3 billion opportunity annually in the United States, which is exciting to us. Not to mention the tens of thousands of lives, we will impact in a positive manner, whether it's from an infection or saving a life. And as Laura said earlier, saving lives and limbs is one of our key models. And I can tell you, that is one of the things that we talk about every single day. Every patient matters, every life matters, every limb matters. Hopefully, that answers your question.

Ryan Zimmerman: Congrats on the progress.

Laura Niklason: So again, I'll probably take that and then let Jim jump in. Yes, certainly, we have seen with our current approval in vascular injury, we've seen an expansion in sales, as you've mentioned. So we are actively targeting -- continuing to target very busy trauma centers in major metropolitan areas, but also very busy vascular surgery practices who do -- who -- where a fraction of their work is also trauma. So that we're continuing to push very hard. We also -- as we've said before, we have filed an MAA application in Israel, and that's marching along. So that's under active review right now, and we're also looking at other opportunities in the Middle East.

I believe that the uptake in vascular injury is going to continue to grow as we're at different sites. As I've mentioned before on previous calls, occasionally, when a surgeon is using our vessel for the first time, he doesn't want to be using it at 2 in the morning when somebody is bleeding to death. That's not the first time he wants to try our vessel. So the pattern that we're seeing is that surgeons are using it in more cases in the daylight that are somewhat more planned, getting some experience there and then moving over and using it more in trauma. And that's just sort of an organic progression that's naturally occurring in hospitals.

So we're going to continue to push that because everywhere that we seed in a hospital that takes care of trauma patients, that's also going to be a hospital that once we're approved in dialysis is taking care of dialysis patients.

Joshua Jennings: Excellent. And then it's encouraging that I think in the press release earlier in the quarter, the team commented on physicians doing real-world Symvess patient case studies for presentation. And then also, will some of these case studies that will be presented occur at VEITH. Laura Niklason: Jim, do you want to take that? Or you want me to take that?

Jim Mercadante: Sure. Laura, I'm happy to take it. So let me just at least start with part of the question. So VEITH will be an exciting time for us. So we're really excited about it. Put that aside and say, yes, there will be multiple case presentations given by physicians. We tend to don't get into that because those are physician presentations. And certain physicians have put out press releases already about their experience and their adoption of it. And certain ones are waiting to present at [indiscernible] to give their feedback and opinion. But we're getting lots of positive feedback and really successful cases in the United States, and we're excited about that. Laura, you probably have a follow-up, I'm sure.

Laura Niklason: Yes. The other thing that I would mention is that along with onboarding Jim in April, we also onboarded Todd Rasmussen, our Chief Surgical Officer. Having a surgeon on Humacyte's team who has done more implants than maybe any other surgeon in the U.S. of our vessel has been just an outstanding tool for us because it makes surgeons out in the field who've never used the product before.

It makes them more comfortable and also because they're better educated, their outcomes are better. And so it's a virtuous cycle.

Joshua Jennings: And good luck down the home stretch of the supplemental BLA filing.

Jim Mercadante: Well, I mean, we tend not to talk about particular pricing on these calls because a lot of our hospital administrators are listening. But what I can tell you is our average price for Symvess around our list price is about $17,000 a unit. But again, when we're starting a particular health care system out, there could be introductory pricing, there could be evaluation pricing. So a lot of things go into that. And sometimes when you're doing that calculation, kind of dilutes it. But I can tell you moving forward and as each quarter goes on, the ASP tends to get stronger and stronger with the adoption of the product.

So while I can't give you very specific information and there's a reason for that, but hopefully, that answers your question, gives you an idea of where we are and where we're headed.

Christopher Pasquale: Okay. And then as we see revenue stepping up here, it should improve the ability to absorb some of the overhead costs that have been flowing through COGS. So do you expect to have a positive gross margin in the fourth quarter given where the commercial adoption is trending? How should we think about that?

Dale Sander: Yes. The biggest -- this is Dale. Chris, the biggest impact on COGS in terms of unused production capacity is whether we're actually in production at that -- at a particular point in time. We had really great success with our production as we closed out 2025. I think at some point in time, we had close to 9 or 10 lots in a row that passed without failure. Operator: Our next question comes from Henry Ware with H.C. Wainwright.

Henry Ware: This is Henry on for [ RK ] And just going back to dialysis, as you're preparing for the potential launch, how much can you build on the existing hospital relationships and the experience established through trauma? Jim Mercadante: You got it. So great question. We believe that the adoption obviously continues throughout Q4 and 2027 of our current indication. And yes, it will directly in a positive manner, impact our launch when we do get approval for dialysis. And the reason is because the same vascular surgeons that are using, for the most part, 8 out of 10 times, the same vascular surgeons that are using our product today also do dialysis access. It's not seamless at all, but there's a real familiarity with it, and it allows us for a much quicker adoption cycle than it would just coming in fresh.

Laura Niklason: Yes. And with respect to Doctors Roy-Chaudhury and Kossmann, these are outstandingly experienced nephrologists, one from the private sector. Rob Kossmann is the former Chief Medical Officer, Fresenius, and he actually ran all of their dialysis centers in the U.S. for many years. And then Prabir Roy-Chaudhury is also very closely involved with the academic leadership in nephrology and past President of the ASN.

So both of these gentlemen have been actively advising us for probably about the last 6 months, and they've really helped us hone in on some of the things that are going to be important both to Medicare, but also to value-based care organizations that are functioning under the Kidney Care Choices model that is supported by CMS. So in terms of the amount of risk that certain value-based care organizations take on, some of these organizations take on 100% of the risk of cost of -- total cost of care for their dialysis patients.

And so these organizations are extremely focused on improving outcomes so that patients have fewer complications and fewer hospitalizations and drive down total cost of care. But these organizations are also very focused on certain metrics like optimal start, which is a scenario whereby a patient can start newly on hemodialysis and avoid a catheter altogether.

So there are -- we're already partnering closely with leaders, Chief Medical Officers and CEOs of various value-based care organizations to understand what their pain points are and to really create a robust financial model that will help them understand how our vessel can both help their patients and get better outcomes, but also help them meet some of their metrics and drive down total cost of care. And frankly, a lot of these interactions have been facilitated from the advice of Dr. Roy-Chaudhury and Dr. Kossmann. We're also speaking with them about CMS reimbursement and other topics. Henry Ware: And then regarding the V012 study presented at ASN, I guess as follow-up continues, are you collecting any additional data? And do you plan to share any of that publicly?

Laura Niklason: Yes. So we stopped enrolling the V012 study when we met our primary interim analysis endpoint. So we had targeted 150 patients total. We had enrolled 120 by the time we completed our interim analysis. So we've got 120 patients enrolled. We had prespecified with the FDA that we would follow all of those patients through year 2, and we're doing that. So the first year data has actually been written up and is being submitted to a major vascular surgery journal as we speak.

We also -- as I mentioned before, we had -- we've published the 1-year results in the V007 study, and we're looking at publishing additional long-term results in the V007 study, which also compared our vessel to fistula as well in men and women. So I see a number of publications coming out even in advance of FDA approval, I see a number of publications coming out relevant to dialysis access in Phase III trials.

Bruce Jackson: I apologize if I missed this, but what's the status of the BioVascular Pancreas? And are there going to be any public data points coming up here in the future?

Laura Niklason: So the BioVascular Pancreas is still certainly a pipeline project for Humacyte. We actually have a publication that's in press right now on some of our primate work that we've done showing long-term islet survival in an allogeneic primate model. I would say that right now, this quarter and next quarter, we're focused pretty tightly on manufacturing and the sales ramp. So we are continuing to work at a benchtop level on the BioVascular Pancreas. But as a company, I think we're focusing most of our energy on growing the commercial story, making product and making sure that we don't stock out because Jim is selling so much. We don't want to run out.

So we're going to make a lot more. And that's really the primary focus for us right now. The BioVascular Pancreas project is something that I think we'll put more resources into probably next year when we have a little bit more daylight around cash flow, but that's where we are. So we're continuing -- we have a publication, and we're continuing benchtop work as of right now.

Operator: We have reached the end of our question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn the floor back over to Laura E. Niklason for closing comments.

Laura Niklason: Yes. Thank you, operator. This has been such a journey, and I'm just so grateful to the employees at Humacyte and also our investors who have been with us on this long and sometimes arduous journey. I want to emphasize that I believe this is a turning point for Humacyte. The revamped commercial structure has already had an amazingly positive impact in an amazingly short period of time. I think this would not be true if we did not have a good product that works and that physicians like and that saves limbs and saves lives. And I believe that, that's all true.

And our commercial execution now is much better, I think, than it was previously, and we're seeing the dividends of that. So I always say I'm excited on these calls, but I am really excited this quarter, and I think that next quarter and then 2027 are going to have a lot more growth. So stay tuned.

#3123. Done with Debian Linux distros? Try Fedora next – 7 reasons why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

After using a Debian-based distribution, you may find yourself longing for something different. I know exactly what you should try next.

Back when I was constantly distro-hopping, I found it important to have a “what’s next” mentality. That way, I could plan accordingly, instead of jumping in blind. I could prepare myself for the installation, the package management system, the desktop, and other necessary bits and pieces.

Also: Fedora Everything let me build the Linux desktop I actually want

But more than anything, I always found it best to know which type of distribution should be next.

You wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to, say, Gentoo, as the leap in required skills is considerable. You also wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to Debian, since Ubuntu is based on Debian, making it a lateral move. From my experience, when coming from an Ubuntu-based distribution, the best next distro is one based on Fedora.

This statement wouldn’t hold water five years ago because Fedora often required work to get it running properly. Now, Fedora requires no work or effort to get it working out of the box. Hardware support is on par with Ubuntu, modern boot processes are supported, it has an excellent first-boot experience, Nvidia driver support is out of the box, the touchpad works out of the box, suspend and resume work flawlessly, it ships with a newer kernel, it includes built-in support for modern display stacks, and it’s clean and bloat-free.

Like many Linux distributions, Fedora lets you choose your desktop, but it does so better by offering dedicated spins for each. You’ll find Fedora spins for KDE Plasma, Xfce, Cinnamon, Mate-Compiz, i3, LXQT, LXDE, SOAS, Sway, Budgie, Miracle, Plasma Mobile, and COSMIC. Instead of manually installing your desktop of choice, just download the Fedora spin with your desired desktop.

Also: Fedora 44 made me forget I was using Linux – in the best way

Yes, there’s a Debian-based distribution for every desktop, but knowing you can just go to the Fedora Project Spins page and quickly find what you’re looking for makes the process easy. As well, Ubuntu has its own “flavors” (such as Kubuntu, Lubuntu, etc.), so coming from an Ubuntu flavor will make total sense.

When using a Debian-based distribution, if you install/manage software from the command line, you’re used to APT, such as sudo apt install quillmark. Did you know that Fedora’s DNF works in the same way? That’s right: sudo dnf install quillmark will get you the same results as sudo apt install quillmark (so long as the app is found in the Fedora repositories).

The same holds true for removing software. One difference, however, is that when system software is upgraded, you’ll have to reboot a Fedora-based distribution for the upgrades to take effect. The only time you have to reboot on a Debian-based distro upgrade is if the kernel is upgraded in the process.

If you’re using Ubuntu as your Debian-based distribution, you’ll find that it includes a universal package manager, just as Fedora does. On Debian, the package manager is Snap, while on Fedora it’s Flatpak. While these two are different, they do have some similarities, such as app installation.

Also: 5 of my favorite Linux distros for AI – and why

With Snap packages, the installation goes something like this: sudo snap install quillmark. On Fedora, that command would be flatpak install quillmark. You’ll notice that sudo is not used with Flatpak; the reason for this is that Flatpak apps are typically installed on a per-user basis. Yes, you can install them system-wide, but that defeats the purpose of sandboxing.

Both Fedora and Ubuntu are secure, even if they arrive at that security by different routes. For example, Ubuntu has AppArmor and Fedora has SELinux. However, both of these tools manage Mandatory Access Controls — just in different ways. The good news is that you’ll probably never have to touch either system.

Also: Ubuntu 26.04 vs. Fedora 44: After years of testing both, here’s my verdict

Also, both Debian- and Fedora-based distributions tend to ship with a GUI frontend for the firewall. If you don’t find one installed, you can install one through your package manager. It is important to know that the Fedora firewall manager is considerably more powerful than Ubuntu’s, which also means it has a steeper learning curve. The good news is that, out of the box, you probably won’t have to make many changes to the firewall, other than ensuring it’s enabled.

Once upon a time, I would have debated such a statement, but Fedora is now on par with Ubuntu in terms of user-friendliness, especially if you choose one of the more user-friendly spins (such as KDE Fedora, Cinnamon, or MATE-Compiz). Fedora also has a System Settings app similar to Ubuntu’s; each one lets you manage nearly every aspect of the computer, so there’s no need to use the command line with Fedora (unless you want to).

With Debian, the release cycle is every 2 years, and support is 5 years. With Fedora, the release cycle is every 6 months, and support is 13 months. If you’re using an Ubuntu-based distribution (which is based on Debian), the release cycle is the same as Fedora, but there are two versions: LTS and interim. LTS support is considerably longer than interim releases: LTS releases receive 5 years of free support, while interim releases receive 9 months.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me

In the end, the Fedora release/support cycle is faster and simpler.

Because both development teams focus on building a user-friendly distribution out of the box, migrating from a Debian-based to a Fedora-based distribution is seamless. When making such a transition, aside from a few minor differences, you’ll feel like you never left your Debian-based distro, especially if you choose a Fedora Spin that includes the same desktop you’ve been using.

#3122. Google Fi’s ‘Super Network’ Hops Networks to Keep Your Pixel Phone Connected

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Automatic network switching for Pixel phones could mean fewer mobile dead zones.

Even in areas that seem abundant with overlapping cellular coverage, phones sometimes sputter when you’re looking up information or trying to get directions when your carrier’s signal gets weak. To avoid those annoying interruptions, Google Fi Wireless is rolling out what it’s calling a “super network” feature. It automatically switches your phone between two 5G networks to maintain the best connection.

The new capability works only on Google’s phones, starting with the Pixel 9 and newer Pixel models.

The super network is included free for existing Google Fi customers on all of its plans: Flexible, Unlimited Essentials, Unlimited Standard and Unlimited Premium.

Google says that it’s using “two top 5G networks,” but the company is refusing to reveal which networks those are in the US. Traditionally Google Fi runs on T-Mobile’s network.

The network switching also applies when you’re traveling internationally, and is included in the Unlimited Premium and Flexible plans.

According to a source at Google, the phone will use two eSIM slots to switch between networks, but it will appear to only use a single eSIM on the customer’s phone. A fine-print disclaimer notes that any other eSIMs on your device must be disabled, which is worth knowing for anyone that already uses multiple carriers on a single device.

In addition to the super network news, Google said its Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus feature is available in millions of more locations across the US. If the phone is in an area where cellular is spotty and a compatible Wi-Fi network is nearby, it automatically makes an encrypted connection if the Wi-Fi network is stronger.

Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus is available on Pixel phones, but is also becoming available on Samsung phones running One UI 9 or later and “select modern Motorola phones.”

#3121. Your FitBit Versa and Sense smartwatches will lose some features this month – what to know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Time's running out for some Versa and Sense models. After Nov. 28, you can no longer install or update third-party apps or clockfaces on these Google smartwatches.

If you have a Fitbit Versa or Fitbit Sense smartwatch, you’ll soon be unable to update the third-party apps on these devices. Google announced on Monday an update to its older lineup of devices that may signify the beginning of obsolescence. Users can no longer install or update third-party apps or clocks on these Fitbit smartwatches, beginning on Nov. 28.

Also: Google’s Fitbit Air is a $99 screenless wearable that I can actually take seriously

The apps will continue to work after that date, but if users delete any of these apps, they will not be able to reinstall them. The changes affect the Fitbit Sense and Fitbit Sense 2, as well as the Fitbit Versa, Fitbit Versa Lite, Fitbit Versa 2, Fitbit Versa 3, and Fitbit Versa 4.

Google noted that users will still have access to Fitbit- and Google-developed apps and clocks, and that they should update to the latest app versions to keep those apps functioning properly.

The Nov. 28 support cut-off comes right on the heels of this season’s Black Friday sales. (Google’s Pixel Watch 5 just got a $100 discount at Amazon.)

So the smartwatches aren’t dead — they can still perform the same primary functions, like recording workouts or receiving or responding to messages and calls. Still, the news is a downer for Versa and Sense users who’ve been using their smartwatches and the many third-party apps on them for anywhere from two to eight years now.

All signs point to these devices being slowly phased out in favor of Google’s latest lineup of fitness trackers and smartwatches.

Also: Google’s new Fitbit Edge solves my biggest gripe with the Pixel Watch

Within the past few years, Google has unveiled an impressive new lineup of health trackers, including the screenless Fitbit Air, the screened Fitbit Edge, and the Pixel Watch 5. For those looking to ditch their Versa or Sense, a few affordable options exist in the ecosystem to take their place.

The earliest and most recent Fitbit Versa models were launched in 2018 and 2022, respectively, and the first and last Fitbit Sense models launched in 2020 and 2022, respectively — making the oldest of these devices eight years old.

#3120. Spotify’s AI DJ adds nine voices and a setting to reduce interruptions

Spotify today expanded customization options for its AI DJ, allowing users to choose between different voices and personalities, as well as control how much the DJ talks between songs. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with Spotify’s AI DJ feature, the company describes it as “a personalized mix of music and commentary to help you discover new favorites and connect more deeply with the artists you love,” adding that it takes your listening history into account to “[bring] together your favorite tracks, songs you haven’t heard in years, and new releases to keep things feeling fresh.”

Spotify first introduced the interactive version of DJ in May 2025, and soon expanded its capabilities to Spanish-speaking users. Then, last May, Spotify expanded availability to more than 75 countries, alongside support for French, German, Italian, and Brazilian Portuguese.

Now, as spotted by TechCrunch, Spotify is introducing more customization options, including new voices and personalities, as well as the ability to reduce commentary between songs.

In a new post published on Spotify’s For the Record blog, the company announced today that “Spotify Premium listeners in markets where DJ is available can choose from an expanded selection of DJ voices in English and Spanish,” with seven new English options spanning British, American, Irish, Australian, and Indian accents, along with two new Spanish voices.

Additionally, Spotify now lets users choose whether they want commentary between sets of songs through a toggle that reduces the DJ’s interruptions to brief acknowledgments when starting a session or requesting different music.

#3118. Gilat Satellite (GILT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Commercial softness offset defense gains as launch delays reshaped the outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Gilat Satellite Networks Ltd. (GILT -20.45%) is undergoing a strategic shift toward defense-oriented revenue streams as traditional commercial markets face structural headwinds, launch delays, and customer delivery changes. Management reported that significant growth in the defense segment and improved profitability in Peru partially offset revenue declines in commercial satellite communications and terrestrial infrastructure projects. The company is currently seeking regulatory approval for the acquisition of Comtech Satellite and Space, an initiative intended to expand its United States market presence and increase defense-sector participation.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for standing by. Welcome to Gilat's Third Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded November 10, 2026. By now, you should have all received the company's press release. If you have not received it, please view it in the News section of the company's website, www.gilat.com. I would now like to hand over the call to Mr. Sanjay Hurry of Alliance Advisors IR. Mr. Hurry, would you like to begin, please?

Sanjay Hurry: Thank you, Hilla. Good morning, everyone. With us on today's call are Mr. Adi Sfadia, Gilat's CEO; and Mr. Gil Benyamini, Gilat's Chief Financial Officer. Before turning the call over to management, I would like to remind everyone that some statements made during this conference call contain forward-looking statements based on current expectations. Actual results could differ materially from those projected as a result of various risks and uncertainties.

The potential risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially include uncertain global economic conditions, reductions in revenues from key customers, delays or reductions in U.S. and foreign military spending, acceptance of our new products on a global basis and disruptions or delays in our supply of raw materials and components due to business conditions, global conflicts, weather or other factors not under our control. The company cautions investors to not place undue reliance on forward-looking statements, which reflect the company's analysis only as of today's date. The company undertakes no obligation to publicly update forward-looking statements to reflect subsequent events or circumstances.

Further information on these factors and other factors that could affect Gilat's financial results is included in the company's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including the latest quarterly report. In addition, on today's call, management will refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures that management considers to be useful and differ from GAAP. These non-GAAP measures should be considered supplemental to corresponding GAAP figures. With that, I would like to turn the call over now to Gilat's CEO, Adi Sfadia. Please go ahead, Adi.

Adi Sfadia: Thank you, Sanjay, and good day, everyone. Thank you for joining us today to discuss Gilat's third quarter 2026 results. Overall revenues for the third quarter was $116.2 million compared with $117.7 million in the same quarter last year. Adjusted EBITDA reached $17.6 million, up from $15.6 million in the third quarter of 2025, a 13% increase year-over-year. For the first 9 months of 2026, revenue reached $349.4 million and adjusted EBITDA reached $48.1 million. Importantly, despite the softer revenue environment, we delivered double-digit growth in adjusted EBITDA and expanded our adjusted EBITDA margin to approximately 15%. This reflects our focus on profitability, a favorable revenue mix and a benefit of our ongoing cost reduction and efficiency initiatives.

Our Defense business continued to demonstrate strong momentum with revenues growing 53% year-over-year, reinforcing the strategic direction we have been pursuing over the past several years. In parallel, our Commercial business is facing some challenges. Our Commercial segment revenues declined to $69.8 million (sic) [ $69.7 million ] compared with $73 million in the same quarter last year, mainly due to lower amplifiers delivery to certain LEO customers that were deferred to later periods. Our updated revenue outlook reflects evolving market dynamics and timing consideration across traditional Commercial segments. In the GEO market, continued expansion by LEO constellation providers is shaping the competitive environment for our customers.

At the same time, longer decision-making process for large satellite projects and the timing of GEO and LEO satellite launches, including launch availability constraints are affecting the pace of satellite deployments and rollouts. As a result, some anticipated orders and revenues are now expected to materialize in 2027 and beyond. In IFC, we are engaged in ongoing negotiations with key customers on commercial terms and conditions aimed at improving our business economics. Coupled with changing customer delivery and installation schedules, new orders are delayed and revenues are shifted into 2027 despite our significant order backlog.

In Peru, an agreement originally expected to be signed at the first half of 2026 was signed at the end of the third quarter, shifting the associated revenues into 2027. In contrast, our Defense business continues to gain momentum and to deliver strong revenue growth, exceeding our expectations. In light of these dynamics, we are updating our full year guidance. We now expect revenues in the range of $455 million to $475 million. The impact on adjusted EBITDA is much more modest, thanks to cost-saving initiatives we have implemented and a favorable revenue mix. As such, we are narrowing our adjusted EBITDA guidance to between $61 million to $63 million.

A few years ago, we anticipated the change is now occurring in the Commercial market. We have been aggressively preparing by shifting our focus and investment to Defense, beginning with the acquisition of DataPath in 2023. We are building on this strategy with pending acquisition of Comtech Satellite and Space business, which we expect will significantly expand our Defense business, strengthen our position in the U.S. market and broaden our technology portfolio. We expect Comtech to add more than $180 million in revenues and more than $80 million in adjusted EBITDA.

The closing of the transaction is still subject to remaining U.S. regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions, which we expect to receive before the end of the year with closing targeted right after. Now on to the business review. I will start with the Defense. During the third quarter, Gilat Defense strengthened its market position, driven by increasing demand for multi-band mobile, rapidly deployable SATCOM solutions that give users resilience and greater flexibility in scaling the relocating network assets to achieve operational continuity on the battlefield. Specifically, Gilat DataPath received an award of more than $32 million for multi-band DKET systems supporting U.S. Defense network resilience.

We are also advancing our DKET multi-orbit capabilities to give Defense customers greater operational flexibility. Gilat DataPath is advancing DKET certification for its transportable gateway systems for operation of both the U.S. Department of War, WGS Network and SES' Empire Sovereign Network. This builds on existing technology and creates an additional growth opportunity for Gilat Defense. We also announced additional orders of more than $8 million from the U.S. Department of War for field services and SATCOM solution upgrades. During the quarter, we achieved an important technology milestone by successfully demonstrating an AI-based capability that detects and cancels interference on satellite links. This innovation supports reliable communication in increasingly complex satellite environments and reflects our ongoing investment in advanced technologies.

Overall, our Defense business continues to build momentum. These awards deepen our relationship with the U.S. Department of War and reinforce our position as a trusted provider of advanced SATCOM solutions for complex operational environment. Turning to Commercial. Our performance reflects both competitive pressure in traditional markets such as enterprise and cellular backhaul and delays in customer programs as discussed earlier. During the quarter, we received more than $10 million in additional SkyEdge IV orders from a leading satellite operator. During the third quarter, we delivered more than 150 Sidewinder ESA terminals.

In parallel, we have entered into ongoing negotiations with key customers to secure more favorable revenue -- sorry, more favorable economic terms for Gilat, and we expect this delay to delay some orders and revenues to 2027 and beyond. At the same time, our customers continue to add new airline to their backlog, and we expect additional orders in line with their installation needs in 2027 and beyond. Longer term, we are also making good progress certifying our multi-orbit Sidewinder ESA terminal as a line-fit solution with Boeing and Airbus. This program is expected to expand our margins and strengthen the profitability of the Sidewinder business over time with delivery of the first units expected before year-end.

We are also investing in our integrated solutions and digital inclusion offering, which integrates connectivity, complementary technologies and platforms to deliver end-to-end essential digital inclusion programs. We are advancing in several large opportunities, and we are very optimistic about the potential this represents for Gilat. Lastly, we also see opportunities developing with several large HTS and VHTS satellite expected to launch in late 2027 and onwards. Our Peru business continued to build on its extensive experience deploying, upgrading and operating large-scale integrated solutions and telecommunication networks throughout the country. During the quarter, we announced 2 significant projects. First, we signed a $28 million contract with Pronatel to upgrade the broadband network in the Ica region.

Ica represents the fifth regional broadband network upgrade awarded to Gilat since 2025. We also signed a $14 million agreement for digital inclusion project. The project will extend broadband access to schools, health care facilities and other public institutions in underserved communities, improving access to essential services. The experience provides a strong foundation for pursuing additional opportunities in Peru and elsewhere in the region as governments invest in connectivity and digital development. During the quarter, we announced a private placement of $100 million in 5-year convertible notes. The financing give us additional flexibility to pursue organic and inorganic opportunities, particularly in Defense and Space, while funding the technologies and capabilities needed to support our ambitions in these markets.

Gilat is navigating changes in the commercial satellite market while transforming its business mix and focus, expanding its Defense operations and placing greater emphasis on growth and profitability. In closing, the third quarter reflects both opportunities and challenges in our evolving markets. Competitive pressure, longer decision-making process and GEO and LEO launch delays, customer delivery changes and ongoing commercial negotiations have shifted revenue timing and have affected our revenue outlook. We are actively addressing these challenges while making clear progress on our long-term strategy. Our Defense business is growing with a 53% increase year-over-year in revenues. Our profitability continues to improve, and we are investing in technologies and capabilities that we believe will support our future growth.

The Comtech acquisition represents a major step in our transformation, adding meaningful scale to the business and further strengthening our position in the U.S. Defense and Space markets. At the same time, we remain focused on capturing opportunities in next-generation ground infrastructure, IFC, new HTS, VHTS and NGSO satellite constellations and integrated connectivity solutions. We recognize the importance of delivering on our commitments and providing greater visibility as this initiative progress. Our priority remains clear: to build a stronger, more diversified and more profitable Gilat positioned for sustainable long-term growth. And with that, I will hand over the call over to Gil Benyamini, our CFO. Gil, please go ahead.

Gil Benyamini: Thank you, Adi. Good morning and good afternoon to everyone. I would like to remind that our financial results are presented both on a GAAP and non-GAAP basis. I will now walk through our financial highlights for the third quarter of 2026. Our third quarter results demonstrate the continued transformation of our business mix, strong growth in Defense, higher gross margins and disciplined cost management drove 13% increase in adjusted EBITDA and approximately 2% of margin expansion despite slightly lower revenue. In terms of our financial results, revenue for the third quarter were $116.2 million, representing 1% decrease compared with $117.7 million in Q3 '25.

The revenues for the Commercial segment in Q3 '26 were $69.7 million compared with $73 million in the same quarter last year. 4% decline year-over-year was primarily driven by lower amplifiers deliveries to certain customers that were deferred to later periods. Revenues for the Defense segment in the third quarter of 2026 were $36.9 million, 53% higher than $24.1 million in the same quarter last year, primarily driven by transportable product deliveries at Gilat DataPath. Q3 '26 revenues for the Peru segment were $9.6 million, 54% lower than $20.6 million in Q3 '25. The decrease mainly reflects lower construction revenues from the upgrade projects, as well as hardware-related delivery revenues recognized in the same quarter last year.

Our GAAP gross margin in Q3 '26 was 35% compared with 30% in the same quarter last year. The increase compared to Q3 '25 is mainly attributed to a more favorable deal mix in the Defense segment as well as improved profitability in Peru. GAAP operating expenses in Q3 '26 were $32.9 million compared with $27.2 million in Q3 '25. The increase was primarily attributable to changes in the U.S. dollar versus Israeli shekel exchange rate, Comtech Satellite and Space transaction-related expenses and a provision for bad debt due to 2 customers entering into Chapter 11 in the U.S. As a result, GAAP operating income was $7.9 million compared to $7.5 million in Q3 '25.

GAAP net income in Q3 '26 was $8.7 million or a diluted income per share of $0.11 compared with GAAP net income of $8.1 million or diluted income per share of $0.14 in Q3 '25. The increase in net income was primarily driven by the higher operating income, while diluted income per share declined due to the higher share count mainly related to equity raises that we did. Turning to non-GAAP results. Our non-GAAP gross margin in Q3 '26 was 36% compared with 32% in Q3 '25. The increase is primarily attributable to the Defense and Peru segment. Non-GAAP operating expenses for the quarter were $27 million compared with $24.7 million in Q3 '25.

The increase mainly reflects the impact of the U.S. dollar versus the Israeli shekel and approximately $1.3 million of bad debt expenses, partially offset by lower R&D expenses, which decreased mainly due to higher R&D grants and NRE expenses related to revenue-generating projects reclassified to cost of revenue. Non-GAAP operating income in Q3 '26 was $14.6 million, 14% higher than the $12.8 million in Q3 '25. Non-GAAP net income in Q3 '26 was $14.3 million or a diluted income per share of $0.18 compared with a non-GAAP net income of $11.8 million or income per share of $0.19 in Q3 '25.

Adjusted EBITDA reached $17.6 million, 13% higher than Q3 '25 despite lower revenues, reflecting a favorable business mix and our cost efficiency initiatives. Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to approximately 15% compared with approximately 13% in Q3 '25. For the first 9 months of '26, adjusted EBITDA was $48.1 million, 37% higher than the same period last year on revenue growth of 11%. Moving to the balance sheet and cash flow. During the quarter, we generated approximately $4.3 million in operating cash, mainly reflecting significant collections from customers in the Commercial and Defense segment, partially offset by working capital buildup related to revenue recognized in Defense with collection expected in subsequent periods.

During the quarter, we also completed the issuance of $100 million 5-year convertible notes with net proceeds of approximately $99 million. We ended the quarter with a strong liquidity position of $260 million comprised of cash, cash equivalents and short-term deposits. Net of the convertible notes and short-term loan, our net cash position was $158 million compared with $157 million at the end of the second quarter this year. DSO were 111 days, excluding Peru construction activity and remained within our expected range. Our shareholders' equity as of September 30, '26 totaled $555 million compared with $545 million on June 30, '26.

Looking ahead, based on our third quarter results, backlog and current visibility, we're updating our full year '26 guidance. Revenues are now expected to be between $455 million and $475 million, representing 3% growth year-over-year at the midpoint compared with our previous range of $500 million to $520 million. The update mainly reflects lower order intake expected in Q4, resulting from delays in GEO and LEO launches, rescheduled IFC deliveries and timing of Peru agreements, which shifted revenues into 2027 in future periods. We're narrowing our adjusted EBITDA guidance to between $61 million and $63 million, representing 17% growth at the midpoint.

The impact on adjusted EBITDA is considerably more limited than our revenues, supported by favorable deal mix and the cost-saving initiatives we've implemented. This outlook continues to absorb the impact of the unfavorable movements in Israeli shekel versus the U.S. dollar on our operating expenses. The updated outlook does not include any contributions from pending Comtech Satellite and Space acquisition. That concludes my financial review. We would now like to open the call for questions. Operator, please go ahead.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question is from Ryan Koontz of Needham & Company.

Ryan Koontz: I want to ask about the Commercial pushouts here, maybe starting with IFC. Is this related to new versions that are lower cost rolling out? Or you're trying to secure some pricing adjustments? Or can you give me some context of kind of what's driving the pushouts from your IFC customers?

Adi Sfadia: Sure, Ryan. So generally speaking, we see some installation delays that shifted some of the deliveries to 2027. In parallel, as we said in the last several meetings, the profitability on the retrofit units are limited and close to breakeven. We would like to ensure that we will make profits on the retrofit as well. Line-fit will be profitable units, but we would like to make sure that we'll make profits on the retrofit as well. So we are working in 2 fronts. One is a cost reduction initiative that takes much longer time than originally anticipated. And in parallel, we started negotiation with customers to have better economics on the unit price.

Ryan Koontz: Yes. That makes sense. Was there something that changed from -- over the last few quarters? Or this is just continued kind of weak economics here that you thought -- you anticipated would get better over time? Is it...

Adi Sfadia: So we anticipated costing will get better over time, and it take much longer time than expected. We had a tight delivery schedule with our customers that we wanted to make sure that they won't lose business. So we fought hard to deliver what they need on time. And in parallel, recently, we started a negotiation on the new contract terms, which we expect to delay some orders and will push some of the deliveries into 2027 onwards.

Ryan Koontz: Got it. And the Q3 deliveries, were those close to what you expected in terms of volume?

Adi Sfadia: Q3 deliveries are exactly as we expected at the beginning of the quarter and based on our plan. The miss on the Commercial this quarter was mainly related to large LEO project that we are delivering SSPA and because of the constellation rollout delays due to launch availability, the customer wants to push some of the deliveries onwards. We do have the units in inventory and backlog, and it's just a matter of time.

Ryan Koontz: Got it. Great. And the overall kind of upside in gross margin in the quarter here was a nice step-up. This is -- it sounds like it's from Defense mix mainly? Or what would you explain this nice step-up in gross margin in September?

Gil Benyamini: Ryan, it's Gil. So this would be a mix. Majority comes from the Defense section as the Defense is growing, and we saw a very nice growth of 53% in the Defense segment. We enjoy economy of scale, that was part of the upscale in the gross margin. And the second part comes from more profitable products that were delivered this quarter, mainly DataPath transportable products. So it's a mix of both. On top of that, we also gained a higher gross margin in the Peru division compared to last year and last quarter.

Ryan Koontz: Helpful. And maybe on the Defense side there, I know you had announced some collaboration with some optical transport space to ground technologies. Any update there you can provide on those new collaborations and products?

Adi Sfadia: So this is an initiative that we are working on almost 2 years. We had a proof-of-concept. We have units that are delivering what we aim to, and now we are engaged with customers for selling transaction. It will take time, but it's something that we believe can drive DataPath and Gilat Defense future growth.

Ryan Koontz: Great. That's nice to hear. And then maybe on the Chapter 11 customer write-off, what was the time line here? I know the customer filed during the third quarter. Were these for recent shipments? Or was this debt that's been around for a while?

Adi Sfadia: It's -- that has been a while -- not for a while. It's relatively recent, but once the customer files for Chapter 11, we need to estimate what are the chances of collection, and we took a decision to write it off.

Operator: The next question is from Louie DiPalma of William Blair.

Louie Dipalma: You referenced the intensifying competitive pressure. For what end markets are you witnessing the biggest impact from the competitive pressure? Is it mostly specific to enterprise? Or are you also starting to see it on the aviation side? And is that the reason for some of the delays that took place? Because it seems that on the solid state power amplifier delays is more of a timing issue and not a competitive issue.

Adi Sfadia: Yes. So we feel the pressure on -- almost on all Commercial subsegments, especially on the enterprise and cellular backhaul. Over there, we feel a lot of pressure. And because there is a significant delays in GEO satellite launches, there is no -- relatively no new networks that are up for grab. So that's delayed orders. There are still several satellites that are expected to be launched in the second half of 2027 and 2028. So we do expect to see nice orders probably at the beginning of 2027 onwards. We do see also -- especially our customers see also competition on the aero side. But we know that our customers continue to win deals.

Their backlog is increased, and we do expect some large orders in the next few quarters. It's really tied to their installation schedule and the ongoing negotiation about better economics for Gilat in this sense. Now as we see today, also the aero is mainly a timing issue. We have significant backlog of units that we can deliver. And our customer has much more backlog than orders that they gave us. The Sidewinder terminal is their go-to-market on the Ku side, and we believe we'll get those orders. It's just a matter of reaching the right economic terms.

Louie Dipalma: Great. And is everything on track for the Comtech deal to close by the end of the year? And assuming that deal closes, what is the pro forma mix in terms of end markets for Defense versus Commercial versus Peru?

Adi Sfadia: Okay. So yes, first of all, the Comtech deal is on track. We received HSR blessing earlier the year. We are now in process of getting CFIUS approval. We expect to get it before the end of the year and closing will be right after. As for the mix, Gil will give you some greater data. But generally speaking, Comtech is going to add around $180 million of revenues. I would say 70% to 80% is Defense-oriented.

Gil Benyamini: In terms of percentage, so about 10% will be Peru and the rest 90%, each of the Commercial and Defense should be between 40% and 50%, depending on the final classification of all end markets.

Operator: The next question is from Sergey Glinyanov of Freedom Broker.

Sergey Glinyanov: I have a couple of them. What do you think about midterm election results and whether it may impact the Defense business? And if yes, what products are under the risk to your opinion?

Adi Sfadia: The midterm effect, it's a big question. It's -- first of all, it's really, it's early period. We don't really know what will happen, but we remain very confident in the outlook of the U.S. Defense business. Political changes can influence budget priorities and timing, but the need for resilience, secure mission-critical communication continues to increase. The acquisition of Comtech Satellite and Space Communication business will strengthen our position in the U.S. and it'll increase our product portfolio and we'll be in direct touch with the relevant Department of Defense entities together with Gilat existing capabilities. We believe it will continue to grow both on U.S. and globally.

So I think it's really early to say, but it's not changing our plans to invest in the U.S. The budgets in the U.S. are huge. It represents 70% to 80% of the overall satellite communication equipment market globally. And at the end, the overall U.S. budget will stay very big, and it depends on priorities within the budget. We believe that today, everyone understands that satellite gives you the resilience the battlefield needs.

Gil Benyamini: And I would like to add that it looks like most of the effect of the midterm should be affecting the reconciliation budgets and not the core budgets and our products are mainly targeted and acquired by the core budget. So as Adi said, we continue with our plans and hope that we'll see much higher revenues.

Sergey Glinyanov: Appreciate the answer. And also -- now more and more airlines are choosing Starlink as their primary IFC solution. So which is causing a lot of concerns about how demand will be affected across different providers and suppliers? How do you assess this kind of risk?

Adi Sfadia: First of all, it's true that Starlink is gaining market share. But as I said, our customers are also getting new deals and increasing their backlog. I think that the addition of line-fit for the Sidewinder increased the attractiveness of our customers. It's not a market that the winner take it all. I think that we are providing a unique terminal that allowed resiliency between LEO and GEO. There is no such antenna available today in the market. And if you -- we are the alternative for -- our customers are the alternative for Starlink.

And if you don't want to choose Starlink and you want GEO -- LEO resiliency, you need to go with -- at the end with Gilat equipment. And as I said, our customer has significant backlog, and we do expect large orders in 2027.

Sergey Glinyanov: Okay. And the last question relates to, is there any update on your Airbus line-fit?

Adi Sfadia: Yes. So we are progressing with both Boeing and Airbus line-fit. We expect Boeing certification to end before the end of the year and Airbus right after. We expect to deliver first unit to Boeing before the end of the year, and Airbus will follow.

Operator: The next question is from Chris Quilty of Quilty Space.

Christopher Quilty: I just want to start off with maybe a macro question on the antenna market, specifically the IFC antenna market and lots of changes there. What are you seeing in terms of technology trends, whether it's single orbit or multi-orbit, either frequency bands, Ku or Ka or a move from the sort of large LEO providers to some of the smaller constellations? Are there opportunities in the LEO market where a lot of them typically just bring the antenna with them?

Adi Sfadia: So, what we see today in the market, today, there is a Ka and Ku and you have the GEO-LEO play or the Starlink only LEO play. If you want GEO-LEO, you need to go with the Sidewinder terminal. What we see in the future based on discussion with players in the market is that the multi-orbit probably will stay. If it will be GEO-LEO or MEO-LEO, it's still under discussion. Definitely, terminals that will be able to connect both to Ku and to Ka on the LEO side will have better chances to succeed, and this is something that the direction that we are working on. We have started the initial development of such antenna.

This is what we are seeing in the market today. I believe that the Sidewinder still has a few hundreds, if not more than 1,000 units to be sold in the next 3 years.

Christopher Quilty: Got it. And switching gears, I mean, on the GEO satellite order side and launch situation, I haven't read the Airbus or Thales press releases, but did they announce further delays on the satellite delivery? Or is it looking more like launch delays?

Adi Sfadia: I think it's mainly connected to launch delays. You saw SpaceX announcement on Falcon 9. I think that Amazon is delaying a bit, Telesat is delaying a bit. So I think that the bottleneck right now is on the launch availability.

Christopher Quilty: Got you. And Gil, I guess, either a question or a request. I mean as the Comtech acquisition closes, if you can provide sort of the pro forma numbers there for us, that would be helpful as we do out the modeling for '27 and '28.

Gil Benyamini: Yes, sure. We will provide all the required data to the investors, and we're also anticipating to provide pro forma and Comtech acquired business on a solo basis as well. We'll do it after.

Christopher Quilty: Got you. Do you also intend at that time to provide update forecast both for the business and for '27?

Gil Benyamini: We'll do it together with Gilat guidance at the beginning of February '27.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The next question is from Gunther Karger of Discovery Group.

Gunther Karger: I know that the expectation of closing the Comtech acquisition is by the end of the year. Is there anything specifically that's holding it up? Or is it basically on track?

Adi Sfadia: It's basically on track. Besides some customary closing condition, we are waiting for CFIUS approval. We already received CFIUS approval in 2023 for DataPath and in 2025 for Stellar Blu. So we don't see a problem with that. It's just a process that we believe will conclude before the end of the year.

Gunther Karger: But specifically, with regard to the government area, the CFIUS, is there any holdup there? Or is that basically also on track?

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. Mr. Benyamini, would you like to make a concluding statement?

Gil Benyamini: I want to thank you all for joining us to the call and for your time and attention. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter. Thank you very much, and have a great day.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes Gilat's third quarter 2026 results conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may go ahead and disconnect.

Expanded Gemini Intelligence, HiLight and more

Google just announced its November Pixel Drop, which adds a slew of new features for Pixel phones and watches. Plus, the Pixel Tag officially goes on sale today (look out for our review here).

There's a ton of stuff in the drop, but some highlights include expanded Gemini Intelligence, a new Create My Widget feature and step-by-step workouts on Pixel Watch 3 and newer.

The company also announced its new Google Fi "Super Network." We've got more details about how it works here.

Let's dive into what's available and which devices support these new features.

For the most part, the big features are only coming to the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series phones in this update. Some smaller tools are available on Pixel 6 and later phones. Surprise, most of it is AI-related.

Starting with AI, Gemini Intelligence is now available on Pixel 10 phones, including the new Rambler feature, which automatically removes filler words and can format your spoken words into "clean, coherent" text. It also adds automations for specified apps, including grocery ordering, ridesharing and booking reservations.

Create My Widgets enables you to build custom widgets using AI by describing the type of tool you need. Google is also offering curated recommendations.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Gemini Call Screen is on Pixel 11 phones and screens calls on demand. For Pixel 10 and 11 phones, Gemini can make calls for you, doing things like checking inventory, putting items on hold, or making/changing reservations.

Pixel 11 phones are getting Pixel Solver, which uses generative AI to create custom templates and "conversational, multi-step problem solving for everyday" math.

Pixel 9 and above phones are getting Notification Summaries that will recap long conversations, giving you context at a glance.

The highlight feature, pun intended, is HiLight, announced at the Made By Google event in August. When your phone is face down, HiLight will glow to let you know if a favorite contact has sent you a message.

Otherwise, for 6a and above, there's a new Custom Icons style, which uses Nano Banana to generate. Transit Mode 2.0 triggers automatically based on phone sensors.

Pixel Search Updates lets you find content across your apps, web and settings using natural language search directly from the All Apps screen.

Unit Conversion is a module to help you skip toggling between the browser and the calculator. Pixel 6 and above phones are also getting Live Location Sharing for Pixel VIPs.

Finally, Pixel 10 phones are getting Extreme Charging Mode that quickly charges your phones to full.

Your Pixel Watch isn't getting as many features as the phones, but the big one is "Step-by-Step Workouts." Basically, your watch will give you step-by-step instructions for each exercise in your routine. It will also log reps, weights and track metrics from your Watch, or your phone.

This is available on Pixel Watch 3 and newer models.

Google announced that Create My Widgets, Gemini call Screen and Notification Summaries, outlined above, are "coming soon"; no specific date was provided.

Phone to Watch Unlock is also coming soon to Pixel Watch 3 and new models. This feature will let you unlock your watch with a nearby paired phone. No date was provided here either.
