#3088. Ring cameras go mobile as Amazon debuts AI-powered security drone and robot

Amazon’s roaming Ring Robotics devices will debut in late 2026 and early 2027.

The Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to plan patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture.

Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration.

The AI Pilot can supposedly use that guided- or self-tour information to identify specific rooms and suggest patrol points near side doors, windows, or even sensitive locations such as a cash register in the case of a business.

Amazon’s Ring Drone appears to be a direct successor to the company’s Ring Always Home Cam that was only temporarily available for purchase by invitation as a “Day 1 Edition” product in September 2021—even having the same starting price of $250.

But the Ring Drone still requires authorization from the Federal Communications Commission before going on sale. Assuming that comes through, Amazon aims to make the drone available on January 27, 2027, with customers able to register for email updates through the product page.

Onboard camera capability includes a 148-degree field of view and 360-degree rotation with a 2K video resolution. Two LED lights also activate in low-light conditions to help illuminate the scene for the drone video camera.

However, the drone is limited to just 8 minutes of flight time when operating on a “new, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions” according to the product description. It comes with a docking station for charging.

Another caveat in the product description is that the Ring Drone Cam may experience degraded performance when navigating in environments with reflective surfaces such as “polished marble or wet tile,” blank matte walls without any features, or transparent surfaces like frameless glass and mirrors.

Still, Amazon touts the drone as providing an “autonomous way to check on your home that has never existed before,” whether the customer is away or at home. The Ring Drone can be controlled directly from the Alexa Home Map interactive map that shows all of a customer’s Amazon-linked devices.

Meanwhile, Amazon has pitched the Ring Rover Cam priced at $1,000 as “an autonomous security robot designed for business.” This product is already available for preorder for those so inclined and scheduled to start shipping to customers on December 16, 2026.

The company described the Ring Rover as being inspired by customer feedback involving another invite-only beta product, the Amazon Astro robot designed for home monitoring.

The Ring Rover can livestream and record in up to 4K video resolution when patrolling or while doing a 360-degree scan at a designated location. Videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and “Live View” events are stored in the cloud for sharing and replaying for up to 180 days.

Like the Ring Drone, the Ring Rover can automatically respond to alerts from connected Ring devices by following its preprogrammed patrol points. But the wheeled robot is only designed to operate within a single-floor, indoor environment because it lacks stair-climbing capability.

Amazon’s product description also warns that the Rover is not compatible with “curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), and black glossy floors.”

To help compensate for its ground-based view, the Ring Rover comes with an automatically adjustable mast to peer over counters, shelving and other obstacles. It can supposedly cover up to 5,000 square feet (465 square meters), according to Amazon’s product description.

The Ring Rover also comes with additional security-related features such as a siren and light tower to loudly announce its presence, along with a microphone for two-way audio communication if the customer wants to address someone near the robot.

Ring was previously charged in a 2023 Federal Trade Commission investigation with allowing employees and contractors to watch Ring video recordings of customers’ private spaces. The FTC also described Ring as having lackluster safeguards that allowed hackers to access 55,000 US customers’ accounts.

Videos taken by the new Ring Drone and Ring Rover will be protected with Ring’s Throw Away the Key Encryption that was introduced in September 2026, according to Amazon’s announcement. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has described this as an improvement over Ring’s former default settings, but still well short of end-to-end encryption.

There is currently no mention of the new Ring Robotics products implementing facial recognition or similar AI-powered technologies for identifying people. But starting in December 2025, Ring has allowed owners of fixed Ring doorbell cameras to turn on a “Familiar Faces” feature that uses facial recognition technology on visitors—and that is already the subject of a class action lawsuit.

Booking a hotel via The Edit leads to instant benefits like free breakfast, property credits, and early check-in and late checkout. While the rates may not always be the lowest you’ll find online, the perks that come with The Edit may more than outweigh any cost differential.

The Edit’s curated collection of hotels and resorts covers a broad range of high-end properties, and the program is only open to select Chase credit cardholders. Don’t forget about the $500 in built-in credits that come with your card, which renew each year and only further the value with Chase’s The Edit program.

#3086. The Overlooked AI Trade Hiding in a Beaten-Down Corner of the Market

Consulting stocks have slumped this year on fears that AI will replace them. But the newest jobs report shows companies hiring consultants at the fastest pace in nearly two years.

Investors have spent 2026 betting that artificial intelligence will put consultants out of work. Through Tuesday's close, Accenture (ACN +1.63%) was roughly flat this year, Cognizant (CTSH +2.20%) was down 20%, and Infosys (INFY +1.61%) was down 31%. Others have fallen just as hard: EPAM Systems (EPAM +4.67%) and research firm Gartner (IT -1.10%) are each down about 20%. Fueling the declines, investors have worried that if AI can write code and analyze data, companies will need fewer people to do it and fewer outside firms to manage it.

But recent jobs data tells a different story.

Employment in U.S. management and technical consulting rose by 17,300 in October to about 1.9 million, according to preliminary Bureau of Labor Statistics data. That was the largest monthly gain since December 2024, bringing the year-over-year increase to about 46,000 jobs, or 2.5%.

LPL Financial thinks AI is the reason. "Companies are not simply spending on chips, servers, and data centers, they are also hiring specialized workers who can help integrate new technology into existing workflows," it wrote in a market commentary this week. It compared the trend to the late 1990s, when consulting jobs grew at double-digit rates as businesses adopted the internet.

In other words, buying AI is the first step, but making it work inside a bank, hospital or factory takes people.

Accenture, the biggest name in the group, is still growing, just slowly. In its fiscal year ended Aug. 31, revenue rose 6% to $74.2 billion, and it set a record with 141 client bookings of $100 million or more. The company employs about 814,000 people, a reminder of how much of this business still runs on people. Fourth-quarter new bookings, a measure of future work, rose 4% to $22.2 billion, and the company expects revenue to grow 3% to 6% this fiscal year in local currencies, with earnings per share of $14.39 to $14.81, up 6% to 9%.

At nearly $260 a share, Accenture trades at roughly 18 times the midpoint of this year's earnings forecast, a modest price for a business that still grows and returns so much cash.

Still, the company is honest about the risk. In the same release, it warns that AI "could harm the company's business, including by reducing demand for our services." And the middle of its growth forecast, about 4.5%, would be slower than last year's 5% in local currencies, a sign that clients haven't rushed into big new AI projects yet.

The market and the jobs data are pointing in opposite directions, and one month of hiring doesn't settle the debate. But if LPL is right that the next phase of AI is about putting it to work, today's beaten-down consulting stocks could be the overlooked winners. Investors who want AI stocks beyond chipmakers may want to start with Accenture and watch whether its bookings keep climbing.

#3085. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

VA mortgage borrowers are quietly navigating a knowledge gap. Here’s how to close it.

If your understanding of a VA home loan starts and ends with “it’s for the military,” you’re not alone. For many eligible veterans and service members, the intricate workings (and benefits) of this U.S. government-backed mortgage are obscured behind lackluster guidance.

While there are classes and resources available, the military is broadly wary of steering members in a specific direction, says Alex Rodino, a real estate agent and U.S. Army veteran who served 10 years as an infantry officer and military advisor. “A lot of the course material is just very generic,” he says.

And that’s not a surprise. Considering the sheer size and scope of the military, providing personalized advice on VA loans to all its members would be no easy task.

That leaves real estate agents and lenders as the last line of defense, which is where a big part of the knowledge gap exists. Rodino purchased his first home in 2020 with a VA loan and says he didn’t like how ignorant he felt during the process.

“The reason I actually got my real estate license to begin with was because of that experience I had,” Rodino says. “Looking back on it, I had a lot of questions that didn't really get answered.”

But how can VA borrowers navigate this knowledge gap without having to become mortgage experts in their spare time? Here are some of the most important things to know when considering a VA loan, according to the financial experts and borrowers who have lived it.

“My mortgage broker said, hey, you might qualify for this, look it up,” says Elizabeth Valente, a real estate investor and former U.S. Army officer who bought her first home using a VA loan in 2021. When it came to the application process, she felt crucial information wasn’t readily available to her or fully explained.

In hindsight, Valente says, working with an agent or lender who had detailed VA loan experience would have been beneficial. Not only would it help untangle the specific paperwork and appraisal requirements, but that expertise offers an important layer of support for military borrowers.

“For some processes in the military, it's very hand-holding,” Valente says. “I'll tell you what to wear, what to bring, when to be there.” But that’s not always true when transitioning back to civilian life, and parsing specifics of a loan process can be challenging. “I don't think a typical Realtor would understand what that person's going through,” Valente says.

Finding professionals with the right expertise involves asking questions — and lots of them.

“If I'm the smartest person in the room, we have an issue,” Valente says. “Don't be afraid to tell someone if something doesn't make sense or if you don't understand the numbers.”

Before agreeing to work with a lender or mortgage broker, ask how their process works, what companies they work with, and how familiar they are with VA loans. Treat the initial conversation like an interview — you’re hiring them, not the other way around.

Knowing where to find your Certificate of Eligibility (COE) and how much you might be eligible to borrow is the responsibility of the person applying, Valente says. “All that information — it is available in the [VA] website but you really have to dig for it.”

And this information isn’t recreational reading — your COE lists your "basic entitlement," which is a crucial figure in VA lending. If you have full basic entitlement, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) generally guarantees 25% of the loan, which in most cases lets you put 0% down.

Why? With a quarter of the loan guaranteed by the VA, the lender is more protected and thus more willing to forgo a down payment.

So how do you know if you have full basic entitlement? Look for the figure $36,000 on your COE. This dollar amount represents full entitlement. Technically, basic entitlement is for loans up to $144,000, but then your bonus entitlement kicks in and you can go higher. The VA doesn’t set loan limits when you have full entitlement — though your lender will still decide how much you can borrow based on your income, debts, credit and the home’s appraised value.

Let’s say you want to buy a home in Fayetteville, North Carolina, and you need a $200,000 loan. In order to put no money down, your entitlement needs to cover at least 25% of the loan amount — in this example, that’s $50,000. After you purchase the home, your COE will show your basic entitlement as $0 and the entitlement charged to a previous loan as $50,000.

“Serving in the military is a unique investing opportunity that most people don't get,” Rodino says. “I wish someone had told me to buy a house when I got to my first duty station.”

If he’d known it was possible or understood how, Rodino says he would have been able to buy in 2017, move in 2020, rent out his first home and then repeat the process. “I'd have three by now and the first one would probably be paid off.”

This particular plan is partly based on the unique schedule of many military members. “Generally, you're moving anywhere from two to four to six years,” Rodino says. Owning multiple properties also leverages two big (and often misunderstood) perks of the VA loan: It’s possible to have more than one active loan at the same time, and after one year, you may be able to convert your primary residence to a rental.

Let’s go back to Fayetteville, North Carolina. After two years, you decide to rent out the home because you’re moving to Bell County, Texas. The home you want to buy in Bell County is $300,000, and in order to make no down payment, you need the VA to guarantee 25% of the loan ($75,000).

Because you no longer have full basic entitlement — remember, you already have an active VA loan elsewhere — your entitlement is capped at 25% of the conforming loan limit in the county where you plan to buy, minus what’s already being used on your first loan ($50,000 in our Fayetteville example).

Now for the math: The current conforming loan limit in Bell County is $832,750. Multiply this figure by 25% and subtract the $50,000 already in use: You have $158,187.50 of entitlement available to you — plenty to guarantee the $75,000 needed on the new loan.

If all of this sounds overwhelming, you’re not wrong. There are resources out there to help you figure all of this out, Rodino says. “The problem is, they're not always practical or they're not always apparent.”

The VA has a website that can walk you through entitlement calculations, but you should also ask your lender, broker or agent. If you’re working with experienced folks, they’ll be able to explain these details and help you get the most out of the VA’s guarantees.

The key takeaway is this: While each VA loan must initially be for a primary residence, borrowers can leverage their entitlement to build an investment portfolio without needing to cough up large down payments.

But these examples don’t consider all of the factors that go into approvals. Like most mortgages, your income, debts and assets dictate your eligibility. And although the VA doesn’t impose credit score minimums, most lenders do — NerdWallet's analysis shows 620 is a common floor.

It’s also important to note that a VA loan’s 0% down isn’t free. VA loans carry a funding fee based on how much you’re putting down and whether it’s your first or subsequent use (certain disabled veterans are exempt). You can pay this up front at closing or roll it into the loan amount; again, your team of professionals should be able to walk you through your options.

“I think there's the assumption that this is what we do: We get our VA home loan and we go buy a home,” says Julie Soares, financial readiness director for the Wounded Warrior Project. When we’re given access to a benefit that offers discounts and perks, it can be hard not to take advantage of it. But this is why financial awareness is critical.

There are a lot of conversations happening right now around homeownership and whether it’s the right choice, especially as affordability remains challenging. So if you haven’t heard it recently, here’s a reminder: Buying property is not the only way to build wealth or create financial security.

“The financial readiness program at Wounded Warrior Project is really leaning into getting further upstream in those conversations,” Soares says. Having a clear understanding of your benefits before you need to use them allows you to make more informed choices.

While it's helpful to understand your entitlement and what you may be eligible to borrow, you don't have to know every little detail about mortgages, or navigate the process alone. Sometimes, the most important thing to know about VA loans is where to turn for help.

If you are unsure of your eligibility or want more information about home loans, you can call the VA's home loans hotline at 877-827-3702.

“Please reach out to Wounded Warrior Project, reach out to the VA, reach out to any service organization,” Soares says. “Not one organization is gonna be able to fix or solve all of these problems. We have to do this as a group.”

#3083. Stock Market Today, Nov. 10: Opendoor Shares Fall on CPI Data Despite Revenue Above $1 Billion

Heavy trading pressured Opendoor as investors weighed the implications of rising consumer prices, today, Nov. 10, 2026.

Opendoor Technologies (OPEN -7.09%), a digital iBuyer platform for residential home transactions, closed at $1.31, down 7.09%. The stock fell as the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed a hotter-than-expected increase in consumer prices, raising the likelihood of further interest rate hikes that will affect home loans. This extended the pressure Opendoor shares already were under after earnings weakness as investors continue to watch housing demand signals.

Trading volume reached 45.1 million shares, coming in about 26% above its three-month average of 35.8 million shares. Opendoor Technologies IPO'd in 2020 and has fallen 88% since going public.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.38%) fell 0.38% to 7,521, while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.74%) lost 0.74% to 25,066. In residential real estate technology, Offerpad Solutions (OPAD -1.86%) closed at $2.11, down 1.86%, and Zillow (Z -5.51%) ended at $28.98, down 5.51%, showing pressure across sector rivals.

Opendoor stock was hit particularly hard today, Nov. 10, due to the government's CPI report, which showed a 0.4% month-over-month increase in overall consumer prices for October, exceeding the 0.3% rise that economists had projected. The surprise data fueled speculation that the Federal Reserve may keep interest rates higher for longer or even consider a larger-than-usual rate hike at its December meeting.

If rates go up, home loans will become more expensive, creating the possibility that the real estate market will weaken, and threaten Opendoor's business growth. Last week, Zillow's third-quarter earnings report conveyed sluggish housing activity via its softer October listing trends, reinforcing cautious housing demand signals across the sector.

This added to Wall Street's concerns over Opendoor's own Q3 earnings results, reported on Oct. 5. The company delivered revenue above $1 billion, up a solid 12% year over year. However, its losses widened -- from a $90 million net loss in Q3 2025 to a $218 million loss this year -- keeping Wall Street’s attention on margin recovery and cash generation in the face of interest rate headwinds for its industry.

#3082. The Stock Market Just Got Bad News on Inflation.

October inflation cooled, but not as much as Wall Street expected, and now investors have to take a half-point Fed hike in December more seriously. That could be a problem for an AI trade that already looks wobbly.

The latest inflation numbers were released this morning. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed prices rose less in October than the month before. Stocks fell anyway, with the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.38%) finishing down 0.4% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.74%) down 0.7%.

The problem isn't that inflation didn't slow; it's that it didn't slow as much as Wall Street expected, and now the market is bracing for a potentially larger-than-expected rate hike in December.

A quarter-point hike was already widely expected. Now investors have to take the possibility of a half-point hike a little more seriously. That could be a problem for an artificial intelligence (AI) trade that already looks quite wobbly.

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.4% from September to October. That's actually down quite a bit from the 0.6% seen the month before. However, economists were expecting 0.3%. Interestingly, for this round there's no year-over-year figure because last year's government shutdown kept the Bureau of Labor Statistics from collecting data in October of 2025.

After jumping 9.1% in September, gasoline prices rose just 1% in October, a welcome change and a major factor in the overall month-over-month decline. Brent crude -- an international benchmark for global oil prices -- dipped below $90 a barrel on Tuesday, which hopefully will help that trend in the months to come.

However, housing costs accounted for more than 30% of October's increase, and medical care and car insurance got more expensive, too. Lower oil prices may be too little too late.

When the Fed held rates steady in October, the most recent jobs report showed the economy had added just 29,000 jobs in September, which helped drive their decision. But that figure has since been revised up to 60,000, and the latest numbers showed employers added another 165,000 jobs in October while the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. The strong jobs data gives less reason to avoid raising rates.

Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.

Before today's inflation reading was released, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he was leaning toward a quarter-point hike. But if core CPI came in around 0.3% again, he said the Fed should consider going a half point. It did just that.

While the market is still betting a quarter-point hike is what the Fed will go with in December, the odds of a half-point raise spiked 11.1% today according to FedWatch.

With further rate hikes likely and sticky inflation keeping longer-term bond yields elevated -- the 10-year U.S. Treasury was up more than 13 basis points today -- borrowing costs for companies are rising.

Lenders have already been asking for a bigger premium on debt from companies involved in the AI data center build-out. That's not likely to change after today's numbers. Expensive borrowing puts a strain on the capital flowing through the system, and if yields get too high, companies may rein in spending. That wouldn't be good for a stock market historically concentrated in a single theme -- AI -- that needs historic levels of investment to thrive.

The airline’s newest lounge will be the second-largest in the network, offering flyers an upgraded experience at Dulles.

You’ll no longer have to go to the basement to get into a United Club at Washington Dulles International Airport.

The brand-new United Club in the new IAD Concourse E spans nearly 40,000 square feet across an upstairs floor and can seat 630 passengers, making it a significant upgrade to the carrier’s existing lounge portfolio at the airport. It’s the second-largest United Club after its newest lounge in Houston, which opened just weeks earlier.

The new lounge by gates E14 and E16 opens to customers Nov. 10, 2026. United invited me to a media preview of the lounge, and here’s what you can expect inside.

The lounge features several nods to D.C.’s iconic landmarks and monuments, as well as the region’s natural beauty.

When you first enter the lounge, you’ll need to scan your boarding pass and then head up the escalators (stairs and elevators are also available) to get to the lounge.

One of my favorite design features as a former D.C. resident is that escalator ride up, which has been recreated to feel like you’re inside a Metro station.

Thankfully, the escalator ride is not as long as at some stations. Looking at you, Dupont Circle!

Once you're upstairs, you’ll walk into the heart of the lounge, with two buffet stations, a centerpiece bar and plenty of seating options, whether you’re traveling as a group or by yourself. (More on food and beverage options later.)

It’s impossible to miss the soaring ceilings in this lounge, especially compared to the bunker-like atmosphere at some of the existing United Clubs.

Don’t forget to look up, where you’ll see a cherry blossom sculpture, an homage to one of the region’s most popular attractions.

There are also two additional lounging areas on both sides of the central area. One is inspired by the Blue Ridge Mountains, which you can see in the distance.

The other has a cherry blossom theme, with light fixtures that branch out from the ceiling.

Massive windows run throughout the lounge, allowing in tons of natural light and offering fantastic views of the airfield. United has a major presence at IAD, so expect to see plenty of United planes.

The United Club has a full kitchen, allowing it to offer upgraded food options compared to its existing lounges at IAD.

You can expect to find sandwiches, salads and hot protein dishes. The lounge also had a ramen bar and a chili bar set up during my visit.

The two buffet stations are located right next to each other, with a dessert station in between.

If you want something to drink, you can head to the bar or one of the hydration stations throughout the space.

There’s plenty of seating at the bar, which has a double archway design. There are also large TVs if you’re trying to keep up with one of Washington’s many sports teams.

The United Club has eight phone booths for those who need to make a call. They’re split between the two lounging areas in the club.

You'll also find a single-stall private restroom, a wellness room, and dedicated men’s and women’s restrooms.

There are no showers in this lounge. To access a shower in a United lounge, you’ll need to head to the Polaris Lounge, reserved exclusively for eligible business class passengers flying on United and select partner airlines.

You can access the United Club by holding elite status, a lounge membership, the right credit card or an eligible premium cabin ticket.

If there’s availability, United sells day passes at the door for flights departing within three hours. You’ll also need a valid same-day boarding pass on a United or Star Alliance flight.

Holding the right credit card is probably the easiest way to get in. United’s most high-end card comes with a United Club membership, while others might offer one-time passes.

If you’re looking for a United lounge, the newest club in Concourse E is where you want to be. It offers more space, lots of light and elevated food options compared to other United Clubs.

Its massive footprint could also ease overcrowding, a common complaint with other lounges.

One thing to consider is location. The concourses at IAD are spread out, and you may need to take a mobile lounge or train to get there. If you want to check out the lounge, make sure you give yourself enough time to get to your gate.

#3080. Only 2 Novembers Since 1950 Have Started Worse for the S&P 500 Than This One. Here's What Followed the Other Weak Starts.

The eight weak starts before this one split evenly. What separated the winters that went badly?

Through Wednesday of last week, November looked OK for the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.38%). The index had climbed roughly 1.4% since its October close. Then it fell 4.36% on Nov. 5, as chip stocks sank on worries that the midterm election results might slow the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

By the close on Friday, Nov. 6, the index was at 7,376.86, down 2.68% from the 7,580.07 where October ended. It has bounced since, to around 7,550 at the close on Monday, Nov. 9.

I ranked every year since 1950 by the same measure, from the last October close through the last close on or before Nov. 7, using Yahoo Finance's daily closes without dividends. Only 2007 and 2008 started November worse.

Both winters went badly. But six other years came close to this one, and they didn't all end the same way.

The index fell 4.76% in the first week of November 2007 and 3.90% in the first week of November 2008. Behind this year's slide, the next six were 1973 (down 2.30%), 1976 (down 2.02%), 1994 and 1951 (each down 1.96%), 1967 (down 1.95%), and 1979 (down 1.92%).

The list depends on how you count the week. End the period a day earlier, on Nov. 6, and 1973 replaces 2007 as one of the two weaker starts. Election Day also used to close the market, so counting the first five trading sessions instead pushes 1976 below this year too, with a 3.21% loss.

From each year's first-week close to the end of the next April, the results were scattered. The index dropped about 15% after 1973, about 6% after both 2007 and 2008, and about 2% after 1976. It climbed roughly 11% after 1994, 7% after 1967, 6% after 1979, and 4% after 1951. Four losses and four gains averaged about zero.

Notably, the typical result has been far better. The S&P 500 climbed over the same stretch in 54 of the 76 years from 1950 through 2025, or about 71% of the time, with an average gain of roughly 6%.

Three of the four losses came with a recession under way or about to begin, going by the National Bureau of Economic Research's dates.

The economy peaked in November 1973, just as that year's weak start played out. It peaked again in December 2007, a month after that year's weak start, and that recession lasted through the entire 2008 case, ending in June 2009.

The fourth year near a recession was 1979. The economy peaked in January 1980, and the index still closed April up about 6%.

The other four years (1951, 1967, 1976, and 1994) saw no recession begin in the next 18 months. Three of them gained, and the only loss was about 2%. Together, the four winters near a recession averaged a loss of roughly 5%, but the other four averaged a gain of around 5%.

Of course, eight winters is a tiny sample, and as a buy-and-hold investor, I wouldn't make much of a first week by itself. And the worst results mainly came in market downturns already under way. The index was around 38% off its record at the end of October 2008, and in 1973 it was already about 10% below the record it set that January.

This year's start came from closer to the peak. The index finished October around 3% under its Oct. 6 record close of 7,818.93.

Just three of the eight earlier years started within 5% of a record. The index rose after 1994 and 1967. But 2007 started closest of all, at around 1%.

Last week's worries focused on tech companies and data centers. As for the wider economy, the latest report looks solid. Real gross domestic product (GDP) rose at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis's advance estimate.

But the advance estimate for the third quarter of 2007 was 3.9%, just before the economy peaked. And the National Bureau of Economic Research didn't name that peak until December 2008.

So the first week has been a bad guide to what followed, but the economy around it has arguably been a better one. Unfortunately, investors tend to learn about the economy last.

Last week's slide might become something bigger, or it could fade by April, like it did in 1994. I doubt this list can show which.

#3079. Nvidia Stock Just Lost 10% in 1 Day. Should You Buy It Before It Reports Earnings on Nov. 17?

The chipmaker usually beats expectations, but the market may be looking for more this time.

Nvidia (NVDA -5.47%) is no longer the most valuable company in the world as of Election Day. Its stock dropped almost 10% in one day, and recent news about CEO Jensen Huang being a possible target of spying sent the stock down even further.The timing here works out to be just one week before Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. Is it a buy ahead of that report?

A swath of stocks took a hit after the election as numerous Democratic candidates who have promised to push for a slowdown in artificial intelligence (AI) development and the AI data center build-out won their races.

Some AI stocks rose on the news, including Amazon, since the market has been worried about the extraordinary amount of money it is laying out on data centers, and investors welcomed the possibility of it slowing its spending spree.

Nvidia, though, benefits from AI spend, which is why its share price dropped so quickly. It's the main provider of the graphics processing units (GPUs) that power AI workloads, with up to 95% of the data center GPU market.

Wall Street expects the company’s revenue to increase 91% this year, and Nvidia management has already provided guidance for a 70% sales increase next year. It called that a "supply-constrained outlook." However, if AI companies are compelled to slow down their build-outs and model development, reduced spending could hurt their chances of making that happen.

For the fiscal third quarter, which ended Oct. 25, management is guiding for about 90% sales growth, and Wall Street expects $2.47 in earnings per share, up from $1.30 last year. Nvidia tends to easily beat expectations, and the stock generally rises after its earnings reports, but not always.

One area the market will be watching is gross margin. Nvidia is guiding for about 74%, but that's lower than recent levels.

NVDA Gross Profit Margin (Quarterly) data by YCharts

That decline is connected to the rising cost of memory chips, which have been plaguing many AI companies.

At the current price, Nvidia stock trades at a low valuation of 11 times next year's expected earnings. If management provides updates that expectations for next year haven't changed for the worse, the stock is likely to rise; a lower P/E ratio usually indicates that the market doesn't think a company can keep growing earnings at a fast rate. If it can, the P/E ratio should rise.

In other words, the market's reaction is likely to take more notice of guidance than results, which are usually stellar.

Long term, Nvidia has an excellent business, and its products remain critical components of AI development, which isn't going away. Now could be a good time for long-term investors to scoop up shares, but expect periods of volatility as AI stocks go through change. And even if you can stomach those ups and downs, at this point, I wouldn't give Nvidia a prime position in your portfolio.

#3078. Prediction Markets Are Arriving in Your Investing App, and That Makes Us Nervous

NerdWallet, Inc. is an independent publisher and comparison service, not an investment advisor. Its articles, interactive tools and other content are provided to you for free, as self-help tools and for informational purposes only. They are not intended to provide investment advice. NerdWallet does not and cannot guarantee the accuracy or applicability of any information in regard to your individual circumstances. Examples are hypothetical, and we encourage you to seek personalized advice from qualified professionals regarding specific investment issues. Our estimates are based on past market performance, and past performance is not a guarantee of future performance.

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. And while our site doesn’t feature every company or financial product available on the market, we’re proud that the guidance we offer, the information we provide and the tools we create are objective, independent, straightforward — and free.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us. This may influence which products we review and write about (and where those products appear on the site), but it in no way affects our recommendations or advice, which are grounded in thousands of hours of research. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews of their products or services. Here is a list of our partners.

Prediction markets are booming, but that doesn’t make them a sound investment strategy.

The investing information provided on this page is for educational purposes only. NerdWallet, Inc. does not offer advisory or brokerage services, nor does it recommend or advise investors to buy or sell particular stocks, securities or other investments.

Around this time every year, we conduct NerdWallet’s annual broker review process. We assess what’s changed in the industry, discuss which brokerage features matter most (and which ones now matter less), and finally, we do the work by opening accounts to test them.

Prediction markets, which have made their way into some of the most popular investing apps, came up more than we expected in testing this year.

At first, we decided to simply collect information on who does and doesn’t offer access to them, without intending to reward or penalize a broker either way. It would be a neutral presentation of facts, not something that would factor into how we scored a broker.

But one afternoon, all together in the office, we confronted an uncomfortable question: “Do prediction markets, and such easy access to them within an investment app, go against NerdWallet’s editorial house views?”

After careful consideration, we all agreed: they do.

So we started to configure our 2027 rubric with a firmer stance against this trendy feature, penalizing brokers that actively market sports and entertainment event contracts, and whose prediction markets come with few, if any, guardrails.

We’ve distilled our discussion down to three main points:

These products are being marketed alongside investments.

We fear they could be discouraging long-term investing.

Let’s start here: Many aspects of trading could be seen as gambling-adjacent. Options, futures, highly leveraged single-day equity bets and even crypto can all easily fall into the “highly speculative” category. So why are we picking on prediction markets in particular?

In our view, a key differentiator is a much lower barrier to entry with few in-app guardrails in place.

Most of the products we mentioned above require some level of fluency — and at times even permission from the broker — to dabble in. To trade options, for example, you need to answer questions about your investing proficiency, your finances and more. And even after approval, the terminology required to trade can be so intimidating that the language itself can become an indirect deterrent.

Event contracts, which form the backbone of prediction markets, are largely presented in the vernacular, and our testing showed approval to trade them is completed with a few taps from the home screen. Moreover, their content is often unrelated to finance — according to a May 2026 report by the Pew Research Center, around 80% of volume on the prediction market platform Kalshi was for sports events[1]Pew Research Center. Trading Volume on Prediction Markets Has Soared in Recent Months. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources .

Answering a binary question (yes/no; this/that), posed in everyday language about a familiar topic — something like, “Will the Knicks beat the Spurs on Sunday?” — can be far less daunting than figuring out what an options chain is or understanding forex pairs.

In other words, what makes prediction markets accessible to a wider audience is also what makes them problematic, especially when housed within an investing account. Which brings us to our next point.

On the platforms that feature them, we found that prediction markets almost always appear alongside stock and ETF trading. We think this is a mistake. What has made these mobile-first investing apps so good for so long (making it easy to move, manage and invest money through a beautiful interface) is what’s now making us nervous.

For example, most investing platforms let users do any number of smart things with idle cash. They could open an Individual Retirement Account (IRA), a custodial account or a robo-managed portfolio all through a single app. But now, they can dip into that same pot of money to bet on whether Beyoncé or Alicia Keys will play the Super Bowl halftime show.

But is anyone actually trading these event contracts? Let’s use data from publicly traded brokers that offer prediction markets to explore this.

In Q3 2026, Robinhood’s revenue from event contracts rose more than 600% year over year to $173 million, while the number of event contracts traded grew more than sevenfold to 16.4 billion[2]Robinhood. Robinhood Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources . This was the second-highest source of transaction revenue behind options trading. In a forecast reported on by Cointelegraph, Bernstein analysts projected Robinhood’s prediction markets could drive $1.7 billion in annual revenue by 2028[3]Yahoo Finance. Bernstein Sees Robinhood Prediction Markets Reaching $1.7 Billion in Revenue by 2028, Topping Crypto. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources .

Coinbase's Q1 2026 quarterly report called prediction markets “one of its fastest-scaling products ever, driven by strong retail interest[4]Coinbase. Coinbase Q1 Financial Results Show Resilient Financial Performance Driven by New All-Time High Crypto Trading Volume Market Share. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources ."

In a call discussing Webull’s Q2 results, U.S. CEO Anthony Denier noted trading volume in Webull’s nascent prediction market product grew about 70% quarter over quarter[5]Gloom. Webull (BULL) Q2 2026 earnings call transcript. Accessed Nov 3, 2026. View all sources .

Gemini’s Q2 report shows prediction market volume rose 93% quarter over quarter[6]Gemini. Shareholder Update Q2 2026. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources .

So, now that we’ve established that these markets are growing in popularity — and investing platforms appear to have a large incentive to lean into them — how are all those event contract traders faring? That brings us to our final point.

Is all this even worth it? Several studies show how hard it is to actually turn a profit in prediction markets. Here are a few:

One study, conducted by researchers at ESSEC Business School, HEC Montréal and the University of Toronto's Rotman School of Management, covered 2.4 million Polymarket accounts across $67 billion in trading volume between November 2022 and March 2026, and found that 69% of users lost money[7]SSRN. Who Wins and Who Loses In Prediction Markets? Evidence from Polymarket. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources . Moreover, the top 1% of users who made a profit accounted for about 76% of all gains. Translation: Even if you did turn a profit, there’s a good chance you didn’t make much.

A Bloomberg analysis supports this: From January 2025 to April 2026, more than 100,000 Polymarket accounts lost at least $1,000[8]Bloomberg. Most Prediction Market Traders Are Losing Money While Bots Rack Up Gains. Accessed Nov 3, 2026. View all sources . Of the 2 million active wallets studied, almost half made or lost less than $10 during the period, while far fewer accounts collected larger profits.

A separate Wall Street Journal analysis echoed the same trend: 67% of Polymarket profits go to 0.1% of accounts, and more than 70% of Polymarket users lost money[9]The Wall Street Journal. Why Almost Everyone Loses—Except a Few Sharks—on Prediction Markets. Accessed Nov 3, 2026. View all sources .

While there is far less data available on Kalshi trades (Polymarket runs on a public blockchain, making it easy to extract and analyze data), a Kalshi spokesperson confirmed in the Wall Street Journal analysis above that one month of data in 2026 showed there were 2.9 unprofitable users to each profitable user[10]Wall Street Journal. Why Almost Everyone Loses—Except a Few Sharks—on Prediction Markets. Accessed Nov 10, 2026. View all sources .

The first study above discusses how event contract trading is binary and zero-sum: If one trader wins, another loses. This means traders allocating money to these instruments could be missing out on aspects of equity markets that have helped create long-term wealth for previous generations.

“Unlike equity markets, there is no equity premium, no dividends, and no passive investment options. Their short maturities naturally encourage short-horizon trading, which is precisely what the behavioral finance literature has suggested is most destructive to wealth accumulation. Given the rapid growth of these platforms and their role as a potential entry point for young investors, understanding who bears the losses has direct implications for investor welfare and market regulation.”

As a reminder, the vast majority of Polymarket users bore the losses.

At NerdWallet, our mission has always been to help people make smarter financial decisions, so we’re sticking by that. Starting with our 2027 ratings, brokers that offer easy access to sports and entertainment event contracts will lose points in our scoring system because we believe this new product has the potential to harm long-term wealth building and doesn’t belong in investing platforms.

So, what’s a better way forward? Bring back the friction and make prediction markets a separate app. Financial institutions, businesses and individuals can still explore legitimate use cases for prediction markets, such as forecasting and hedging. And we’re not here to stop anyone from trading event contracts for entertainment with extra money. We just don’t want these markets so easily conflated with the legitimate investing vehicles these apps already offer. And our reviews will reflect that.

#3077. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.
