#3041. Stock Market Today, Nov. 10: Wall Street's Rally Hits a Roadblock as Hot Inflation Raises the Stakes for the Fed

Yesterday's rebound lost momentum as rising Treasury yields and renewed inflation concerns weighed on stocks

Wall Street's rebound stalled on Tuesday, November 10, as hotter-than-expected inflation data reignited concerns about Federal Reserve interest rate policy and sent Treasury yields higher. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.74%) dropped 0.74% to 25,066, retreating from Monday's gains, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.38%) slipped 0.38% to 7,521 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -0.30%) fell 0.30% to 52,232.

Selling pressure extended beyond equities as gold fell 1.84% to $4,038.70, while the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.88%, approaching the psychologically important 5% threshold. Market performance was mixed across sectors, with consumer cyclical stocks leading gains and industrials advancing, while healthcare lagged. The divergence highlighted an increasingly selective market as investors reassessed the outlook for interest rates and economic growth.

Despite the broader market decline, several prominent stocks posted strong gains on Tuesday. Meta Platforms (META +0.00%) surged more than 5% after JPMorgan (JPM +0.00%) added the social media giant to its Focus List, while Sea Limited (SE -1.49%) jumped 8.1% following stronger-than-expected quarterly revenue.

On the downside, Nvidia (NVDA -5.47%) plunged 5.52% amid an ongoing investigation involving CEO Jensen Huang, adding to uncertainty ahead of the chipmaker's upcoming earnings report.

Tuesday's sell-off underscores a growing challenge for equity investors heading into year-end. With inflation proving more persistent than expected, markets are increasingly pricing in another Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Higher borrowing costs could weigh on corporate profitability and put additional pressure on stock valuations, particularly among growth companies whose valuations depend heavily on future earnings.

However, the divergence in individual stock performance suggests investors are becoming more selective rather than abandoning equities altogether. Strong corporate earnings and favorable company-specific developments continue to attract capital, even as broader market conditions deteriorate. This could favor businesses with healthy balance sheets, strong cash flow, and the ability to sustain growth without relying heavily on external financing.

Looking ahead, investors should watch upcoming inflation data, Federal Reserve commentary, and Treasury yields for signs of whether monetary conditions will tighten further. With the 10-year yield approaching 5%, the sustainability of Wall Street's recent rebound may depend increasingly on corporate earnings delivering enough growth to justify elevated valuations.

#3039. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3033. Why Lincoln Educational Services Stock Soared Again Today

Yet another peer just posted an estimates-beating quarter.

For the second trading session in a row, Lincoln Educational Services (LINC +4.54%) stock posted a solid gain on Tuesday. The company's shares continued to benefit from bullish momentum sparked by its impressive third-quarter earnings report and similarly encouraging results from a peer. Its shares closed Tuesday more than 4.5% higher.

That peer is American Public Education (APEI +2.84%). It published its third-quarter results after market close on Monday, and its stock rose the following day. That was mainly thanks to enrollment increases in both of its core operating divisions and to management's top- and bottom-line guidance revisions.

This will sound familiar to Lincoln Educational shareholders, as these dynamics were at play in their company's third quarter. What also helped Lincoln was its double-digit increases in student starts, population, and overall revenue -- and, yes, a guidance raise.

This, along with the recent quarterlies of other education stocks, suggests that demand is rising for the vocational and specialty learning services these companies provide.

To me, two key factors are contributing to that demand. The first is the shortage of skilled trade and technical workers in the U.S. This has been caused, in large part, by several generations that have placed a premium on "traditional" college and university degree programs over vocational learning. The second is the ever-rising cost of such programs, which has made them harder to afford for many Americans, particularly amid rising consumer prices.

These feel like durable mid- to long-term trends, as I don't see the causes behind them melting away anytime soon. I think the education sector will continue to post encouraging growth, and I'd consider its better stocks to be buy candidates -- Lincoln Educational included.

#3029. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3028. Jensen Huang’s 700,000% Return Magnifies Nvidia Succession Risks

The office of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has an unusual setup: The chief executive officer sits at an enormous oval desk facing his lieutenants, with room for more employees in stadium seating behind them. The arrangement — created as part of Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California — is purpose-built to suit how Huang runs the company. Though it’s not uncommon to see cultlike tech CEOs who obsess over details, Huang is in a class of his own. He has led the business since its very beginning 33 years ago, the longest such run in Silicon Valley. And even as Nvidia grew into one of the world’s most powerful companies — with a stock return of more than 700,000% — there’s still no one designated to potentially replace him. Ian King, Bloomberg News US Semiconductor reporter discusses the latest. (Source: Bloomberg)

#3027. NH Investors (NHI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Senior housing now drives 18% of income, but summer occupancy fell short of plans.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

National Health Investors, Inc. (NHI -4.83%) reported a third quarter defined by the completion of its $541.6 million skilled nursing portfolio sale and the subsequent rotation of capital into the senior housing operating segment. Management indicated that the Senior Housing Operating Portfolio now contributes 18% of total net operating income, doubling its share since the beginning of the year. While the same-store portfolio met growth objectives, recently acquired properties experienced operational delays and occupancy growth that trailed management's initial expectations. The company maintained a leverage ratio below its target range while executing $396.2 million in year-to-date investments, positioning the firm for its second largest investment year in company history.

Operator: Good day, everyone, and welcome to the National Health Investors Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Webcast and Conference Call. [Operator Instructions]. It is now my pleasure to hand the floor over to your host, Dana Hambly, Senior Vice President of Finance. Sir, the floor is yours.

Dana Hambly: Thank you, and welcome to the National Health Investors Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. On the call today are Eric Mendelsohn, President and CEO; Kevin Pascoe, Chief Investment Officer; Todd Siefert, Chief Financial Officer; Chris Maingot, Chief Operating Officer; and David Travis, Chief Accounting Officer. Yesterday, NHI released its third quarter results and conference call information for a press release after market close. Today's remarks may include forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks or uncertainties and are not guarantees of future performance.

Investors are urged to carefully review NHI's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including its Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, and Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, for a discussion of these risks. Copies of these filings are available on the SEC's website at sec.gov or on NHI's website at nhireit.com. In addition, today's call may include certain non-GAAP financial measures, reconciliations of which are provided in NHI's earnings release, which has been furnished to the SEC on Form 8-K. Listeners are encouraged to review those reconciliations provided in the earnings release together with all other information provided in that release. I'll now turn the call over to our CEO, Eric Mendelsohn.

D. Mendelsohn: Good morning, and thank you for joining us. This has been a year of significant transition for NHI. We completed the sale of the NHC portfolio on July 1, substantially reduced our skilled nursing exposure and accelerated our investment in private pay senior housing. Our conviction and SHOP remains strong. We continue to see the most attractive risk-adjusted opportunities for our capital in private pay senior housing, where we believe that the industry backdrop provides powerful and sustained tailwinds for our company. Capturing that opportunity requires both disciplined underwriting and consistent execution. While NHI is focused on the long-term opportunity, we understand the importance of delivering consistent quarterly results.

And in that regard, our third quarter SHOP performance fell short of our expectations. Our 15 same-store properties delivered approximately 19.5% year-over-year NOI growth, consistent with our outlook, but recent performance in the non-same-store communities reduced the contribution we expected from the total portfolio in the quarter. We're not satisfied with those results and are addressing the operating performance with our partners. Our longer-term growth outlook for those properties is unchanged. Chris Maingot, our new COO, will discuss the drivers and our response in more detail. The NHC sale provided $555 million in net proceeds to support NHI's repositioning. We expect to recycle more than 95% of those proceeds before year-end, primarily into SHOP and expected SHOP transition investments.

We've already completed more than $395 million in investments year-to-date and expect significant additional closings during the fourth quarter. Based on that activity, we expect 2026 to be our second largest investment year in the company's history. This portfolio repositioning enhances our growth profile and the portfolio's valuation potential as we redeploy capital from skilled nursing assets into senior housing. By increasing our exposure to SHOP, we participate directly in operating upside and strengthen NHI's long-term growth profile. Including our October acquisition, SHOP now contributes approximately 18% of total NOI compared with 9% entering the year, and we expect that share to grow rapidly as our investment focus is primarily towards SHOP opportunities.

We are executing this strategy from a strong financial position. Our leverage is less than 3x, which is comfortably below the low end of our target range, and we have ample capital available to fund our current pipeline. That flexibility allows us to remain selective to pursue investments that meet our return standards, including low to mid-teens unlevered IRRs. Kevin will provide more details on our investment activity, and Todd will review our financial position and full year guidance. We have also strengthened our executive management team and clarified responsibilities to support a larger operating portfolio.

Chris is leading our asset management team and the build-out of our operating platform, while Kevin is focused entirely on business development and expanding our investment relationship. Together with Todd's financial leadership, this structure gives us greater capacity to grow the portfolio and manage it effectively. We're encouraged by the direction of these changes and our objective remains high single-digit to low double-digit organic SHOP NOI growth. Our priorities are clear: improve the operating performance, deploy capital thoughtfully and build the capabilities to support sustainable growth. We believe the strategy and team are in place, and we recognize that operating results will be the measure of our success.

We are focused on delivering to meet the expectations that we establish and earning your confidence through consistent execution. We have made considerable progress during this transitional year, and I have confidence in the company's strategic direction. I believe NHI is exceptionally well positioned to capitalize on the most attractive senior housing environment that I have experienced in my career. I'm excited about the opportunities ahead. With that, I'll turn the call over to Kevin. Kevin?

Kevin Pascoe: Thank you, Eric, and good morning. I'll begin with our recent investment activity and pipeline, then discuss our business development priorities and the broader investment environment. Year-to-date, we have completed $396.2 million in investments at an average yield of 7.5%. That includes $320 million of SHOP investments at an average year 1 yield of 7.3% after routine CapEx. Our SHOP acquisitions have averaged approximately $223,000 per unit, well below estimated replacement costs, providing an attractive basis for operating growth. We recently completed $51.4 million in investments on 2 properties we previously held $42.3 million in construction loans. Our incremental capital investment was a modest $9 million net of the proceeds of these loan payoffs.

These transactions demonstrate our loan-to-own strategy, allowing us to not only establish strategic relationships during development, but ultimately acquire the completed and stabilized properties. Turning to the pipeline. We currently have $285 million under signed letters of intent, including approximately $190 million that we expect to close during the fourth quarter. Those anticipated closings would bring our total 2026 investment to approximately $590 million. The properties we expect to acquire before year-end will initially be structured under net leases with anticipated conversions to SHOP in 2027. This structure allows us to complete the acquisitions in 2026 within the time frame to our planned Section 1031 exchanges with a clear path for future participation in the operating performance going forward.

Beyond the signed LOIs, we are evaluating approximately $400 million comprised primarily in SHOP. We continue to see active flow of investments and enter 2027 with a substantial pipeline. Our focus is on communities in primary and secondary markets with identifiable opportunities to increase NOI through incremental occupancy gains, pricing growth, expense management and targeted capital investment. We continue to expect high single-digit to low double-digit organic NOI growth, supported by specific operating goals with our operating partners at each property. Existing relationships remain an important source of investment activity. All investments completed year-to-date have been relationship-driven. As our SHOP portfolio expands, we intend to build meaningful scale with select group of operators.

Adding communities to established relationships allows us to leverage prior diligence, supports more efficient asset management and deepens alignment with our operators. Recent interest rate movements have prompted additional discussion and negotiations, although we have not yet seen meaningful change in pricing. If higher financing costs persist, this could moderate competition for acquisitions and make new development more difficult to justify. We believe our access to capital, ability to execute and strong operator relationships position us well as a reliable partner in that environment. We continue to make progress on resolving lingering issues for a subset of the same-store SHOP portfolio where we believe capital could be more productively redeployed. We will provide further details as our plans are finalized.

We are pleased with this year's investment activity and the opportunities ahead. Our priority remains disciplined growth, acquiring communities at an attractive basis, expanding strategic operator relationships and investing where we see the strongest potential for long-term returns. With that, I'll turn the call over to Chris to discuss portfolio performance and our operating initiatives.

Christian Maingot: Thank you, Kevin. It's a privilege to join you today as NHI's Chief Operating Officer. I joined NHI because I believe the company is well positioned to be the capital partner of choice for senior housing operators. Its track record of building long-term relationships, seasoned team, access to capital and growing commitment to SHOP were key factors that attracted me to the company. Over the past 3 months, I've spent considerable time with our team and operating partners getting to know the portfolio. That work has only reinforced my confidence in the opportunity ahead. It has also helped us identify some near-term priorities and opportunities for improvement, which I'll touch on in a moment.

Let me start with our third quarter results. Total SHOP NOI increased 134% through significant contributions from acquisitions over the past 12 months, and the Same-Store portfolio grew NOI 19.5% year-over-year. While the growth was substantial, the quarterly result was below our expectations. Occupancy growth during the summer selling season was slower than we anticipated. It reflected transition-related operating disruptions and slower growth at certain legacy holiday communities. Unusually high onetime expenses at select operators also impacted the quarter. Our immediate priority is improving revenue growth with particular attention to communities where filling vacant units offers the greatest RevPAR opportunity.

We've been working with our operating partners to ensure they have in place fully staffed sales positions, rent-ready inventory, pricing and incentives that align with local market conditions. We also introduced targeted short-term incentives for community teams at select properties to support sales activity. The sequential increase in recurring capital expenditures largely reflected spending to prepare vacant units for occupancy. Having that inventory available is essential to converting tours to move-ins. As we execute on these properties, we see some encouraging signs in occupancy over the past 3 months. Consistent with typical seasonal patterns in senior housing, we expect occupancy to taper as we move through the holiday season.

Move-in incentives and variability in holiday-related expenses may also temper the near-term financial benefit of that progress. At the recently acquired communities, we view these transition-related disruptions as temporary. We continue to believe these investments can perform in line with our underwriting and are working to get performance on the right track. We are currently partnering with our operators to develop the 2027 operating budget and business plans. We entered that process with a clear view of the growth opportunities across the portfolio, the communities that warrant the greatest attention and the actions needed to improve performance. Our approach is tailored to each community and includes identifying revenue-enhancing capital projects and directing resources where we see the greatest potential return.

To support this work, we've also made some changes to our internal organization. We have realigned our asset management team by investment type and functional expertise, establishing separate teams dedicated to SHOP and to triple net and loans with clear responsibilities and expectations for each. Data-driven decision-making will be central to our approach. To support that commitment, we have bolstered our data and analytics team. This team will strengthen our portfolio insights while improving our tools, processes and technologies. By combining community operating data with broader market and customer information, we aim to identify opportunities earlier, work more efficiently and help our team and operating partners improve performance. We are recruiting for several positions to support these efforts.

Over time, I believe this approach can support organic SHOP NOI growth in the high single-digit to low double-digit range. Our priority is improving execution and establishing a more consistent operating trajectory. Turning to triple-net portfolio. The portfolio continues to provide a solid foundation with healthy EBITDARM coverage across the major asset classes. Bickford paid more than $1 million in percentage rent during the quarter, modestly ahead of our guidance assumptions. My first 3 months have only strengthened my confidence in NHI's opportunity. Our focus is on translating that opportunity into consistent operating performance as we grow, and I look forward to doing so alongside our team and operating partners.

With that, I'll turn the call over to Todd to discuss our financial results.

Todd Siefert: Thank you, Chris, and hello, everyone. Let me start by providing details on our third quarter financial results, followed by a brief discussion about our balance sheet and liquidity and conclude with our revised guidance. For the quarter ended September 30, 2026, our net income per share was $11.47 compared to $0.69 per share in the prior year third quarter. The significant increase was driven by a $541.6 million gain on the sale of the NHC portfolio. We also recognized $9.9 million impairment on a property that was held -- classified as held for sale during the quarter and has subsequently been sold in the fourth quarter.

NAREIT FFO and normalized FFO for the third quarter were $1.12 per share, respectively, compared to $1.09 and $1.32 per share, respectively, in the prior year period. NAREIT FFO and normalized FFO for the third quarter of 2026 included $1.1 million in transaction costs related to acquisitions we decided not to pursue. NAREIT FFO and normalized FFO in the third quarter of 2025 included approximately $3.9 million in cash rental income related to lease terminations on 7 properties previously leased to Discovery Senior Living that were not -- were part of our SHOP transition. The third quarter of 2025 also included approximately $9.7 million in rental income from NHC.

FAD for the third quarter decreased by approximately $5.2 million compared to the prior year period. The decrease was driven primarily by the sale of the NHC portfolio and the prior year's Discovery lease termination accounted for approximately $13.6 million of the decline. This was offset by acquisitions completed since the end of last year's third quarter. Our cash rental income of $58.4 million declined by $12.9 million compared to the prior year's third quarter due to the items I just reviewed and other dispositions partially offset by acquisitions completed over the past year. Total SHOP NOI increased by 134% to $11.5 million.

Interest income from mortgages and other notes declined by 20.6% to $5.1 million due to lower outstanding notes receivable balances. We also earned approximately $2.9 million of interest on NHC sale proceeds held for future Section 1031 exchanges. General and administrative expenses for the third quarter increased 26.8% to $8 million compared to $6.3 million in the third quarter last year as the company continues to ramp its SHOP growth strategy, which contributed to a $1 million increase in compensation costs. Legal expense of $1 million consisted primarily of costs incurred on a large SHOP transaction that we stopped pursuing during the quarter, as referenced earlier.

Interest expense for the third quarter decreased 9% year-over-year due to lower average debt outstanding. Turning to our balance sheet and liquidity. Our reported net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio at September 30 was 3.6x. Adjusting for the $340 million available for future Section 1031 exchanges, our net debt to adjusted EBITDA was 2.4x. We have a $100 million private placement note due in January 2027, which we expect to repay by the end of 2026. We have no other debt maturities until 2028. Our available liquidity at September 30 was approximately $1 billion, consisting of $497 million of available revolver capacity, $500 million under our recently refreshed ATM program and cash on hand.

We also had approximately $340 million in restricted cash and deposits held for future qualified Section 1031 acquisitions at the end of the quarter. Regarding the quarterly dividend, our Board of Directors declared a quarterly dividend of $0.94 per share payable January 29, 2027, to stockholders of record on December 31, 2026. As announced last night, we revised our full year guidance to a range of $4.68 to $4.70 per share for both NAREIT and normalized NFFO and $236.6 million to $237.7 million for funds available for distribution.

The revised FAD range represents a $5 million reduction at the midpoint. The revised guidance incorporates approximately $2.3 million in reduced SHOP NOI from the 42 properties in the portfolio at September 30 and increased recurring CapEx of approximately $2.8 million. As Chris discussed, we accelerated certain routine capital expenditures that are supporting occupancy gains. These items are partially offset by stronger performance and expectations elsewhere in the organization compared to our prior guidance. That concludes our prepared remarks. Thank you again for joining us today. Operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question is coming from Juan Sanabria from BMO Capital Markets.

Juan Sanabria: Just hoping you could expand a little bit on what drove the SHOP underperformance relative to expectations? Was it smaller assets, older assets, any particular operators to call out? Christian Maingot: Yes. This is Chris. First of all, great to be here on my first NHI call. Breaking that down a little bit, definitely, it was a revenue issue. I'll put it in 2 different buckets. As it relates to our new acquisitions, in those particular transactions, we did experience operator transitions. And with any operator transition, there tends to be some disruption. I think the disruption here was a little bit more pronounced. We saw some pretty local mom-and-pop type family businesses being sold to more sophisticated incoming operators. And with that, there's a level of complexity as you introduce new technologies and so forth. So the pickup there was a little slower than we expected.

We did see in a portfolio, the incoming occupancy was below where we thought the starting point would be. And then we saw in another portfolio just some immediate move-outs. Ultimately, and I've been to a number of these assets and portfolios, we believe in these deals. We think the long-term business plan is in line with our underwriting. The other bucket I would tell you is that on the Same-Store while the pool of assets performed in line, there is a cohort there that continues to lag that brought down our overall occupancy and our overall variance to forecast. So yes, that's...

Juan Sanabria: Great. And then maybe you could talk a little bit about how we should think about G&A. You've made some additions. D. Mendelsohn: Juan, this is Eric. On the G&A, we're definitely beefing up our operations. As you know, I come from an operations background. So if we're going to do this, we have to do it right. Juan Sanabria: And just as a quick follow-up, that CapEx was originally considered or incorporated into the underwriting and it's just been brought forward? Or is this over and above what you had originally expected?

D. Mendelsohn: I would say it's over and above because of some of the stealth improvements that we've had to do that were not budgeted. Right now, Chris is doing a detailed budgeting process with all the operators so that we don't have any surprises in the future.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Jamie Feldman from Wells Fargo.

Jesus Garcia: This is Jesus on for Jamie. Just kind of focusing on the 11 properties here entering the Same-Store SHOP pool in the fourth quarter. Christian Maingot: The 11 assets, the new incoming assets?

Christian Maingot: Okay. Thanks, Jamie. I think we feel good about -- I didn't hear -- good about the growth of those assets going forward. Fundamentally, they're in line with our view of the kind of go-forward business plan there for -- yes.

D. Mendelsohn: Yes. And part of the strategy of diving into SHOP like this is we buy buildings in markets that are showing a lot of promise that have less competition and the buildings have room for growth. We understand that the market wants high single-digit, low double-digit occupancy. So a lot of our buildings are in the low to mid-80s. So it gives us that upside. Anything to add to that, Kevin?

Kevin Pascoe: Well, I would remind you, too, that one of those is conversion, and we already have unlocked some value out of that from converting it from a lease to SHOP. We still think there's more growth to come. And I think that's a function of what we've seen this quarter is we still expect more, and we believe they'll get there.

Jesus Garcia: That's great, guys. And just on the remaining 1031 redeployment here, can you just talk about like how the exchange deadline is influencing your evaluation of the remaining acquisition opportunities and the progress you're making towards that target?

Kevin Pascoe: Jesus, this is Kevin again. I would tell you that, as Todd said, we are -- we pretty much have those dollars allocated. We feel very good about the assets we have under LOI. Andrew Reale: This is Andrew Reale on with Farrell. You mentioned this focused plan to strengthen SHOP performance. Christian Maingot: Yes. Thanks, Andrew. First of all, moving the line -- moving the top line on our SHOP portfolio is priority 1, probably priority 1, 2 and 3. Coming into this, if I take a look at it in 3 different buckets, from an asset standpoint, our priority immediately was to try to get move-ins. And so we instituted a plan to really just try to make sure that our operators had the nuts and bolts in place, which was, as I kind of mentioned in the opening remarks, do we have salespeople in the buildings? Are we priced appropriately? Do we have vacant rent-ready rooms and then are we incentivizing people? So an initial push to try to get occupancy.

Secondly, we have kind of bifurcated the portfolio into some buckets so that we have a good view of which of the assets we need to lean into, as Eric kind of mentioned on the CapEx front. Where do we want to invest and how do we think about each of the assets and what are the individual levers that we want to pull on those assets in order to get the RevPAR growth that we need to achieve?

Lastly, we're in the process of doing the budgets, and that's critical. Timing is perfect. There, we're building out our 2027 business plan. And with that comes kind of CapEx and some support. We are working with them on those business plans, and we're also evaluating ways that we can work with them in tandem and where we can bring our resources to the table so that we can get joint performance. Andrew Reale: Got it. That's helpful color. And maybe just as a follow-up, in the prepared remarks, you noted some costs tied to a larger SHOP transaction that you chose to stop pursuing. I guess what drove that decision? And how are you thinking about portfolio size opportunities from here?

D. Mendelsohn: We're always -- this is Eric. We're always chasing large portfolios when they're available that makes sense for us. So just a reallocation of our current capital.

Austin Wurschmidt: And then with respect -- could you speak more broadly with respect to the -- I think it was 7 assets that you transitioned in August of last year, how those specifically have performed relative to underwriting following the transition?

Christian Maingot: Thanks, Austin. Yes. A bit of a mixed bag. We've got a few communities that are high flyers that we'll be leaning into, and then we've got some other ones that we're nursing and bringing along. Occupancy has been a little bit more stagnant than we would have liked, but we have seen, again, some pickup here coming out of third quarter.

Austin Wurschmidt: Got it. And then maybe just one last one for Eric. My understanding has been the last 1.5, 2 years has been spent sort of building out the infrastructure internally to prepare for building out SHOP. I guess beyond maybe some of the data and analytics team that Chris talked about in the prepared remarks, what's still missing from the formula to allow you guys to get ahead of some of these challenges that operators and assets are facing and sort of limiting, I guess, the impact it's having on growth on a go-forward basis?

D. Mendelsohn: I'd say we're 75% to 80% there with our hiring. I feel good about the team that's in place. I feel good about the infrastructure. As we add buildings, we'll add asset management. We'll add accounting folks, but that can happen in tandem with the acquisitions. And I'd say we're 80% there on all the hiring.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your next question is coming from Rob Stevenson from Huntington.

Robert Stevenson: Most of my questions have been answered. But just wanted to -- one on the guidance. Is that just redeployment of the remaining NHC proceeds?

Dana Hambly: Rob, it's Dana. I mean the simplest piece is we had the transaction costs in the third quarter. That's $1.1 million. We'll pick that obviously won't repeat in the fourth quarter. And then there were some other puts and takes. I think, obviously, we've talked about SHOP quite a bit. I think we did a little bit better in the triple-net and cumulatively, everything else kind of evens out. But again, we'll pick up a couple of cents in the fourth quarter on just not having the transaction cost.
